docs.title: 1. Download
docs.text:
• Main code: Corpus.download() -> GlossDownloader.download_files()
  • Purpose: read a metadata parquet, expand list/JSON URL cells, deduplicate URLs, download supported file types, and checkpoint progress.
  • Public targets only: credential URLs, signed/token query fields, cookies and credential settings are refused before a request.
  • Typical inputs:
  • a parquet file in input_dir or an explicit input_parquet
  • a URL column such as url or links_column
  • Main outputs:
  • downloaded files in downloads/
  • partial/final results in download_results/
  • Read this next if you want the scheduler details: gloss_downloader.py

docs.title: 2. Extract (Phase‑1)
docs.text:
• Main code: Corpus.prime_extractor(), Corpus.extract(), GlossExtract.ensure_extractor(), GlossExtract.extract_path()
  • Purpose: convert source files to markdown and optional intermediate JSON artifacts.
  • Typical inputs:
  • files already present in downloads/
  • or explicit file_paths
  • Important parameters:
  • phase1_backend='safe'|'docling'|'auto'
  • default auto uses safe PDFium extraction with layout-aware Markdown, without Docling; GLOSSAPI_MARKDOWN_LAYOUT=plain keeps plain text. Docling extraction is an explicit optional layout backend.
  • repair_fonts=True (default): worker-local CPU ToUnicode repair before safe or Docling extraction; False uses the original text layer
  • use_gpus='single'|'multi'
  • workers_per_device to fan out more than one extraction worker onto each GPU
  • export_doc_json and emit_formula_index for later Phase‑2 work (Docling backend only: select phase1_backend='docling'; the safe backend writes neither)
  • Operational note:
  • force_ocr is deprecated and ignored in Phase‑1; use Corpus.ocr(ocr_options=plugin_options) after clean() for OCR remediation
  • Main outputs:
  • canonical markdown in markdown/<stem>.md
  • repaired copies in repaired_pdfs/<stem>.pdf; originals in downloads/ are preserved
  • parquet font_repair_status, font_repair_fonts, font_repair_valid_rate_before and font_repair_valid_rate_after (rates use first 20 pages when GLOSSAPI_GREEK_WORDLIST is configured; otherwise null)
  • every extraction derives the repair from the source again (an existing repaired_pdfs/<stem>.pdf is never reused by modification time); pre-pass errors/timeouts fall back to the original, using the shared file budget (see Extract stage)
  • problematic_files/ and timeout_files/ (debug) are created by extraction for files it could not convert
  • optional Docling JSON and index artifacts in json/ (Docling backend only)
  • per-document and per-page metrics in json/metrics/

docs.title: 3. Clean
docs.text:
• Main code: Corpus.clean()
  • Purpose: run the Rust cleaner, remove low-quality or noisy markdown, and mark documents that may need OCR retry before moving on.
  • Typical inputs:
  • markdown/*.md
  • metadata parquet, if available
  • Important parameters:
  • drop_bad: remove the documents the fixed gates reject (mojibake_badness_score above 0.1, or Greek badness above 60) from downstream selection
  • empty_char_threshold and empty_min_pages for OCR fallback decisions
  • threshold is deprecated and has no effect; passing it raises a DeprecationWarning
  • Main outputs:
  • cleaned markdown in clean_markdown/
  • updated parquet metadata with quality and OCR-related flags
  • Resume state:
  • interrupted streaming runs resume from the ledger (glossapi run --resume RUN_ID); the metadata parquet is the compatibility state the phase methods read and write. No pickle file is written or read.

docs.title: 4. OCR Retry and Phase‑2 Enrichment
docs.text:
• Main code: Corpus.ocr() and Corpus.formula_enrich_from_json()
  • Purpose:
  • OCR the pages page quality routes (page_routing="all", the default, as glossapi run does), or only the documents the cleaner flagged (page_routing="flagged")
  • optionally decode formula/code regions from Docling JSON into markdown
  • Modes:
  • ocr_bad
  • math_only
  • ocr_bad_then_math
  • Main outputs:
  • refreshed markdown/<stem>.md
  • json/<stem>.latex_map.jsonl when math/code enrichment runs

docs.title: 5. Section and Annotate
docs.text:
• Main code: Corpus.section(), GlossSection.to_parquet(), Corpus.annotate(), GlossSectionClassifier.*
  • Purpose:
  • split markdown into sections suitable for classification
  • classify sections and optionally expand coarse labels into full document structure
  • Main outputs:
  • sections/sections_for_annotation.parquet
  • classified_sections.parquet
  • fully_annotated_sections.parquet

docs.title: Artifact Layout
docs.text:
The tree below shows the main folders and files GlossAPI can create under the output directory.

To make the layout easier to follow, artifacts are grouped by the role they play in the pipeline:

  • canonical — the main outputs a stage is expected to produce, and the files later stages usually depend on
  • debug — extra files kept around when something fails or needs a closer look
  • ledger — the provenance ledger and the private work area of Corpus.run() / glossapi run
OUT/
├── downloads/                                  (canonical)
│   └── problematic_math/                       (debug)
├── repaired_pdfs/                              (sidecars: repaired extraction inputs)
│   └── <stem>.pdf
├── download_results/                           (canonical)
├── markdown/                                   (canonical)
│   └── <stem>.md
├── clean_markdown/                             (canonical)
│   └── <stem>.md
├── json/                                       (canonical)
│   ├── <stem>.docling.json(.zst)
│   ├── <stem>.formula_index.jsonl
│   ├── <stem>.latex_map.jsonl
│   ├── metrics/
│   │   ├── <stem>.metrics.json
│   │   └── <stem>.per_page.metrics.json
│   └── problematic_math/                       (debug)
├── sidecars/extract/<stem>.json                (per-document extraction metadata)
├── sections/                                   (canonical)
│   └── sections_for_annotation.parquet
├── classified_sections.parquet                 (canonical)
├── fully_annotated_sections.parquet            (canonical)
├── export.jsonl                                (canonical, written by the export stage of a run)
├── corpus.sqlite3                              (ledger)
├── .glossapi/artifacts/                        (ledger: private stage outputs of a run)
├── problematic_files/                          (debug, extraction)
└── timeout_files/                              (debug, extraction)

Notes: - json/<stem>.docling.json(.zst) and json/<stem>.formula_index.jsonl exist only after a Docling extraction (phase1_backend='docling'). - Enriched Markdown replaces the plain Markdown (single canonical location). - Metrics lived under markdown/ in earlier versions; they now live under json/metrics/. - When math enrichment cannot recover after the configured number of respawns, the corresponding PDFs and Docling artifacts are copied into the problematic_math/ folders above and the stems are added to the fatal skip-list for later review. - The same folder can act as both input_dir and output_dir; the pipeline creates its own subdirectories under that root.

docs.title: Readability Shortcut
docs.text:
If you only need the shortest path through the system:

  1. Corpus.download() if you start from URLs.
  2. Corpus.extract() for Phase‑1 markdown.
  3. Corpus.clean() to decide what needs OCR.
  4. Corpus.ocr() for selective OCR and optional math/code enrichment.
  5. Corpus.section() and Corpus.annotate() for structured outputs.

If you need to jump from these ideas to the source files, see code_map.md.

docs.title: Exporting corpora
docs.text:
Use Corpus.jsonl(...) when you want a single JSONL file (e.g. quick inspection) and Corpus.jsonl_sharded(...) when preparing pretraining releases. Both calls accept the same knobs for renaming the text column, nesting pipeline metadata, and wiring an external source-metadata parquet.

from pathlib import Path
from glossapi import Corpus

corpus = Corpus(input_dir=Path("input"), output_dir=Path("out"))

shards = corpus.jsonl_sharded(
    Path("out/export"),
    shard_size_bytes=500 * 1024 * 1024,
    shard_prefix="train",
    text_key="text",
    metadata_key="pipeline_metadata",
    metadata_fields=[
        "filter",
        "greek_badness_score",
        "is_empty",
        "latin_percentage",
        "mojibake_badness_score",
        "needs_ocr",
        "percentage_greek",
        "polytonic_ratio",
    ],
    include_remaining_metadata=False,
    metadata_path=Path("out/download_results/didaktorika_downloads_enhanced.parquet"),
    source_metadata_key="source_metadata",
    source_metadata_fields=["filename", "language", "handle_url", "date_accepted"],
    source_metadata_path=Path("out/source_metadata/didaktorika_full_enriched_FINAL.parquet"),
)

docs.title: Loading in downstream trainers
docs.text:
Hugging Face Datasets can stream the resulting .jsonl.zst shards without unpacking:

from datasets import load_dataset

dataset = load_dataset(
    "json",
    data_files="out/export/train-*.jsonl.zst",
    streaming=True,
)["train"]

for row in dataset:
    text = row["text"]  # pipeline metadata is under row["pipeline_metadata"]
    break

For analytics or training-time filtering, keep the Parquet sidecars keyed by doc_id (or filename) and use PyArrow predicates:

import pyarrow.dataset as ds

dataset = ds.dataset("out/metadata/source_metadata.parquet", format="parquet")
recent_greek = dataset.to_table(
    filter=(ds.field("language") == "Ελληνικά") &
            (ds.field("date_accepted") >= "2018-01-01")
)

These snippets are mirrored in the test suite so regressions in file layout or compression settings are caught automatically.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This page shows the most common tasks in a few lines each. Every recipe assumes a source install of glossAPI in an activated environment (Onboarding Guide) and names the optional packages and hardware it needs. Install optional packages in that environment with python install_glossapi.py PACKAGE [--device DEVICE]. When you save a recipe as a script file, put the calls under if __name__ == "__main__":: per-document work runs in worker processes started with spawn, which import the script again.

docs.title: Stable (PyPDFium, size‑1)
docs.text:
Core install only; no GPU.

from glossapi import Corpus
c = Corpus('IN', 'OUT')
c.extract(input_format='pdf')  # safe PDFium backend, layout_v2 Markdown; OCR is off by default

This keeps Docling out of the hot path and is the recommended mode when you prioritise stability.

docs.title: Throughput (Docling, batched)
docs.text:
Needs the optional layout package (python install_glossapi.py layout --device cuda126, or cuda132) and a CUDA GPU.

from glossapi import Corpus
c = Corpus('IN', 'OUT')
c.extract(input_format='pdf', accel_type='CUDA', phase1_backend='docling')

phase1_backend='docling' streams multiple PDFs through Docling’s converter and should be used when you are comfortable trading some stability for throughput.

docs.title: Multi‑GPU
docs.text:
Needs the layout package and several CUDA GPUs.

from glossapi import Corpus
c = Corpus('IN', 'OUT')
c.extract(input_format='pdf', use_gpus='multi', phase1_backend='docling')  # workers share a queued file list

Workers report per-batch summaries and extraction progress is persisted into download_results/download_results.parquet, so you can restart multi-GPU runs without losing progress (no extra checkpoint files required).

docs.title: OCR remediation (opt-in)
docs.text:
Needs the ocr package (python install_glossapi.py ocr --device cpu, or mps / cuda126 / cuda132). The default pinned Greek toolkit needs no options.

from glossapi import Corpus
c = Corpus('IN', 'OUT')
c.extract(input_format='pdf')
c.clean()
c.ocr(mode='ocr_bad')  # pinned Greek R8 + x1 toolkit; pages page quality routes (page_routing='all')

docs.title: Phase‑2 Math Enrichment (from JSON)
docs.text:
Needs the layout package (python install_glossapi.py layout --device cuda126, or cuda132) and a CUDA GPU. Math enrichment consumes existing Docling JSON from an explicit Docling extraction. The safe PDFium backend does not create these inputs.

from glossapi import Corpus

c = Corpus('IN', 'OUT')
c.extract(
    input_format='pdf',
    phase1_backend='docling',
    accel_type='CUDA',
    export_doc_json=True,
    emit_formula_index=True,
)
c.formula_enrich_from_json(device='cuda', batch_size=12)  # enriched Markdown into OUT/markdown/<stem>.md

Progress (downloaded, OCRed, math-enriched) now lives in download_results/download_results.parquet; rerun c.ocr(..., reprocess_completed=True) whenever you need to force already successful rows back through OCR or math.

docs.title: Full Pipeline (download → extract → clean/ocr → section → annotate)
docs.text:
Needs the download package (python install_glossapi.py download) for download() and the ocr package for ocr(); the other calls are core.

from glossapi import Corpus
c = Corpus('IN', 'OUT')
c.download(input_parquet='urls.parquet', url_column='url')  # optional: a parquet with a URL column
c.extract(input_format='pdf')        # Phase‑1 (no OCR by default)
c.clean()                            # compute quality; filter badness
c.ocr(mode='ocr_bad')                # default Greek R8+x1 plugin
c.section()                          # to parquet
c.annotate()                         # classify/annotate sections

See OCR & Math Enrichment for OCR runtime details, batch sizes, and artifact locations, and OCR plugin migration for the toolkit pins, caches and the explicit ocr_options of a custom plugin configuration.

docs.title: OCR runs on CPU
docs.text: • Verify Torch CUDA: python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.cuda.device_count())".

docs.title: Torch doesn’t see the GPU
docs.text:
• Check nvidia-smi and driver installation.
  • Match Torch CUDA build to your driver; see getting_started.md for the recommended wheel.

docs.title: Out of memory
docs.text:
• Lower Phase‑2 batch_size (e.g., 8) and reduce inline GLOSSAPI_FORMULA_BATCH.
  • Reduce GLOSSAPI_IMAGES_SCALE (e.g., 1.1–1.2).
  • Split large batches or files.

docs.title: Worker respawn limit reached
docs.text:
• When a GPU crashes repeatedly, the controller stops respawning it after GLOSSAPI_MATH_RESPAWN_CAP attempts. Any pending stems are added to the skip‑list and their inputs are copied to downloads/problematic_math/ (PDFs) and json/problematic_math/ (Docling artifacts); inspect those folders, address the issue, then rerun Corpus.ocr(..., reprocess_completed=True) or move the quarantined files back into downloads/.
  • Check the corresponding worker log under logs/math_workers/ (or the directory set via GLOSSAPI_WORKER_LOG_DIR) for stack traces and the active stem list stored in gpu<N>.current.

docs.title: A script that calls Corpus.run() fails at start-up
docs.text: The stage workers of a streaming run are started with spawn, so each one imports your script again. Put the call under if __name__ == "__main__":.

docs.title: clean is unavailable after pulling new code
docs.text: glossapi capabilities shows the cleaner or noise module as missing with stale native module ...; rebuild core: the installed extension was built from older Rust source. Rebuild with python install_glossapi.py core (add --editable for a checkout) or pip install -e ..

docs.title: A run refuses to start with post_close_edit
docs.text: A corpus copy that the previous run left unflushed (for example export.jsonl) was changed after that run closed. glossAPI keeps your edit and refuses every start until you move or delete the file; it is then republished from the managed source. The CLI reports the typed code post_close_edit (exit 3) with the edited paths in details.paths. See Resumability, recovery and retention.

docs.title: A run refuses with unresolved_recovery
docs.text:
Every product glossAPI manages has one expected state, decided from the ledger alone: the bytes of its newest committed generation, nothing after a committed deletion of that generation itself, or a refusal when no committed generation can be named. A registration is a committed generation only when its producing attempt ended ok and a positive record binds it to that attempt at that path: a publication record of exactly this path, these bytes and this attempt, or the registration itself listed in the attempt's output manifest. Bytes an attempt produced at one path never make it the producer of another path; a second named copy needs its own publication record. A deletion of any other registration of the path (a step's temporary file at the same name, another run's) never removes a product's obligation. A file the legacy compatibility steps only observed is not a managed product only for the allowlisted diagnostic roles (logs, the temporary cleaning report); any other file only a compatibility step registered is refused (unlisted_observation_role). A rollback that undoes a failed attempt records a permanent invalidation of that attempt's registrations; if it cannot restore a product (its only source was released), it records a pending republication instead, which only a newer committed generation of that product discharges.

The refusal comes from one of three places, each with the typed code unresolved_recovery (exit 3) and its details.boundary:

  • a run start (start) or a repeated publication (publication) found a corpus file it must repair (a copy the previous run left unflushed, or bytes a failed attempt put in place) and could not bring it to its expected state: the file is kept as it is and the run stops there;
  • the completion gate (completion): once per run, after the run's final flush and under the corpus lock, every managed product is hashed against its expected state. The run's work has been done, but the run does not report completed: a product that differs (completion_gate_mismatch), is missing (completion_gate_missing), is present where it must be absent (completion_gate_extra), or has no committed generation (completion_gate_refused, for example a pending republication) is named.

Every run start first commits a new validation generation to the ledger (a validation_started record, written durably) before it validates or repairs anything. From that commit on, no earlier pass counts: only a pass verdict for this generation makes the corpus completed again. If even that commit fails, the start stops before any validation or repair and says so (validation_start_unrecorded, "nothing ran"; typed disk_full when the disk or ledger is full); that refusal is still recorded when the ledger can take it, and then every surface reads unresolved_recovery. Only when both the generation commit and the refusal's own record fail does an earlier pass stay current (nothing was validated or repaired by that start). A refusal is recorded as a verdict when the ledger can take it; when it cannot, the error says the refusal was not recorded (details.refusal_recorded: false), and a generation committed at the start still keeps the corpus from reading completed. A pass whose generation or fingerprint is malformed (not a plain integer or null, not a 64-hex digest) never counts (malformed_generation). A run returns completed only when its pass verdict was durably committed; if that append fails, the run fails (completion_verdict_unrecorded, or disk_full).

glossapi status and glossapi report (and a streaming run's status) show a run completed only when its own completion gate passed AND that pass is still current: it is the ledger's latest verdict, it was recorded after the latest run start, it validated the latest validation generation (a pass recorded by a release before validation generations existed never counts: run once more to revalidate), no product was written, deleted, rolled back or invalidated after it, and the ledger's expected state of every product is still the one the gate verified (the verdict carries a fingerprint of that whole expected state, recomputed on every read). After a refusal they show unresolved_recovery (status exits 3); when the gate never ran, validation is pending, or later changes have not been verified yet, unverified. A later run whose gate passes makes the corpus current again. The gate's cost (products, bytes read, passes, elapsed) is part of its verdict event.

details.conditions names each path and its reason:

  • hard_linked: remove the extra hard link.
  • conflicting_locks or lock_mismatch: move or delete the file; it is then republished.
  • path_replaced: the file was replaced by a symlink; remove the symlink.
  • source_changed or no_intact_source: the managed source under .glossapi/artifacts changed or is missing; restore it or use another corpus.
  • contradictory_registrations: the ledger still lists another generation of the file as present; it needs a maintainer (report it).
  • present_after_deletion: the ledger deleted this file by policy but a file is there again; move it away.
  • missing_at_flush, missing, changed_after_flush, changed_after_restore, changed_during_check, flush_failed, recovery_error: the file vanished, changed or could not be read or flushed while recovery checked it (the condition names the error). Check the disk and anything else writing to the corpus, then resume; the check is repeated from the start.

After the cause is removed, resume: the file is repaired and the run goes on. For a gate refusal, resume after removing the cause (or rerun the publication that must replace a product with a pending republication); the gate runs again at the end of that run.

A temporary that an interrupted publication left beside a product (.<name>.<id>.tmp, or a metadata <name>.<id>.tmp) is removed at the next run start (Corpus.run, or a single-phase call such as Corpus.clean()), whether or not that publication is ever repeated, but only when the ledger's record of that publication proves it is the abandoned copy: the exact recorded path, a regular file with one name, holding the recorded bytes or a strict prefix of the recorded source, checked under the lock its writer held. One whose bytes recovery cannot prove to be its own abandoned copy is never deleted and never blocks a run, once the product itself is resolved. It is residue: delete it yourself if you do not need it.

docs.title: conversion.log appears in the working directory
docs.text: Standalone scripts that construct the extractor write conversion.log in the working directory unless GLOSSAPI_CONVERSION_LOG_FILE names another path. Point it outside the checkout for long runs.

docs.title: Where are my files?
docs.text:
• Enriched Markdown overwrites markdown/<stem>.md.
  • JSON/indices/latex maps: json/. Metrics: json/metrics/.
  • A streaming run's ledger: corpus.sqlite3; its document export: export.jsonl; its private stage outputs: .glossapi/artifacts/.

docs.title: API Reference — glossapi.Corpus
docs.text:
The Corpus class is the high‑level entrypoint for the pipeline. Below are the most commonly used methods.

Use this page as a compact contract reference. For the stage-by-stage artifact view, see ../pipeline.md. For the source-level ownership map, see ../code_map.md.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
glossapi.Corpus(
  input_dir: str | Path,
  output_dir: str | Path,
  section_classifier_model_path: str | Path | None = None,
  extraction_model_path: str | Path | None = None,
  metadata_path: str | Path | None = None,
  annotation_mapping: dict[str, str] | None = None,
  downloader_config: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
  log_level: int = logging.INFO,
  verbose: bool = False,
)
  • input_dir: source files (PDF/DOCX/HTML/…)
  • output_dir: pipeline outputs (markdown, json, sections, …)
  • downloader_config: defaults for download() (e.g., concurrency, retries; public targets only, no cookies or credentials)
  • Main side effects: creates the standard output folders and lazy-initializes the extractor, sectioner, and classifier.

docs.title: run()
docs.text:
run(
  files=(),                      # local paths or URLs; empty = every document the corpus already knows
  *,
  stages=('extract', 'clean', 'sections', 'export'),
  workers: dict | None = None,
  settings: dict | None = None,  # e.g. {'debug': 'off', 'memory_saving': 'normal'}
  resume: str | None = None,     # a run_id to resume
  retry_failed: bool = False,
  plan: dict | None = None,      # a saved `glossapi plan --json` body
) -> dict
  • Purpose: one streaming run of the selected stages, recorded in the corpus ledger corpus.sqlite3. Each stage's prerequisites are added (for example export adds extract and clean). glossapi run calls the same code.
  • Returns the run data (run_id, state and counts), the same object as glossapi run --json prints in data.
  • Stage workers are separate processes started with spawn. They import the calling script again, so guard a script that calls run() with if __name__ == "__main__":; without the guard the run fails in a confusing way.
  • resume=RUN_ID restores that run's frozen plan and settings (no other arguments may change them). Interrupted or lost attempts are retried automatically, at most 3 attempts per task; retry_failed=True retries the failed tasks of the resumed run. See Resumability, recovery and retention.

docs.title: extract()
docs.text:
extract(
  input_format: str = 'all',
  num_threads: int | None = None,
  accel_type: str = 'CUDA',        # 'CPU'|'CUDA'|'MPS'|'Auto'
  *,
  force_ocr: bool = False,
  formula_enrichment: bool = False,
  code_enrichment: bool = False,
  filenames: list[str] | None = None,
  file_paths: list[str | Path] | None = None,
  skip_existing: bool = True,
  use_gpus: str = 'single',        # 'single'|'multi'
  devices: list[int] | None = None,
  use_cls: bool = False,
  benchmark_mode: bool = False,
  export_doc_json: bool = True,
  emit_formula_index: bool = False,
  phase1_backend: str = 'auto',    # 'auto'|'safe'|'docling'
  repair_fonts: bool = True,
  workers_per_device: int = 1,
  batched: bool | None = None,
  page_range: tuple[int, int] | None = None,
  ocr_options = None,
) -> None
  • Purpose: Phase‑1 extraction from source files into markdown plus optional JSON intermediates (Docling backend only).
  • Typical inputs:
  • files already present in downloads/
  • or explicit file_paths
  • Important parameters:
  • phase1_backend='safe'|'docling'|'auto': PyPDFium for stability vs Docling for native layout extraction; 'auto' (default) uses the safe backend unless formula or code enrichment is requested
  • repair_fonts=True (default): repair eligible ToUnicode maps into repaired_pdfs/<stem>.pdf before extraction; each call repairs again from the source
  • batched=None (default): cross-document layout batching only for single-device, layout-only Docling on CUDA; CPU, MPS and the safe backend stay sequential
  • page_range=(first, last): inclusive one-based pages, explicit sequential single-device Docling only
  • ocr_options: an external Docling OCR engine's options; sequential single-device Docling only
  • force_ocr: deprecated no-op kept for compatibility; OCR remediation now lives in Corpus.ocr(mode='ocr_bad')
  • use_gpus='multi': use all visible GPUs through a shared work queue
  • workers_per_device: fan out more than one extraction worker onto a single visible GPU when measuring throughput
  • GLOSSAPI_DOCLING_MAX_BATCH_FILES: optional environment override for how many PDFs one Docling worker processes per extractor batch; GlossAPI keeps the default at 1 until a benchmark proves a larger batch is safe on the target node
  • GLOSSAPI_DOCLING_BATCH_TARGET_PAGES: optional environment override for the page budget of each queued multi-GPU Docling work item; use it with benchmark checkpoints when long PDFs dominate the tail
  • GLOSSAPI_DOCLING_PAGE_BATCH_SIZE: optional environment override for Docling's internal settings.perf.page_batch_size; use it when a GPU can hold more pages in flight than the default internal batch window
  • export_doc_json=True: write json/<stem>.docling.json(.zst) (Docling backend only; the safe backend writes none)
  • emit_formula_index=True: also write json/<stem>.formula_index.jsonl (Docling backend only)
  • Main outputs:
  • markdown/<stem>.md
  • json/<stem>.docling.json(.zst) when enabled with phase1_backend='docling'
  • json/metrics/<stem>.metrics.json
  • json/metrics/<stem>.per_page.metrics.json

clean(

  • Typical inputs:

  • metadata parquet if present

docs.text:
ocr(
  *,
  fix_bad: bool = True,
  page_routing: str | None = None, # None = "all" for the OCR modes, "flagged" for math_only
  mode: str | None = None,
  backend: str = "docling",
  ocr_options = None,
  device: str | None = None,
  max_pages: int | None = None,
  limit: int | None = None,        # accepted, no effect
  dpi: int | None = None,          # accepted, no effect
  math_enhance: bool = True,
  math_targets: dict[str, list[tuple[int,int]]] | None = None,
  math_batch_size: int = 8,
  math_dpi_base: int = 220,
  use_gpus: str = 'single',
  devices: list[int] | None = None,
  force: bool | None = None,       # deprecated alias of fix_bad
  reprocess_completed: bool | None = None,
  skip_existing: bool | None = None,  # deprecated; use reprocess_completed
  content_debug: bool = False,
) -> None
  • Purpose: selective OCR retry and optional Phase‑2 math/code enrichment.
  • Mode selection (without mode, fix_bad and math_enhance choose it: both → ocr_bad_then_math):
  • ocr_bad: OCR the selected pages (see page_routing)
  • math_only: run enrichment from existing Docling JSON; performs no OCR
  • ocr_bad_then_math: OCR first, then enrich the documents OCR did not touch from existing Docling JSON
  • Page selection (page_routing):
  • default "all", the page policy of glossapi run: every page that page quality routes is OCRed, in documents the cleaner flagged and in documents it did not
  • "flagged": OCR only the documents the cleaner flagged (needs_ocr), the default before K4g
  • mode="math_only" performs no OCR and by default still skips only cleaner-flagged documents

  • Important parameters:
  • mode, fix_bad, page_routing, math_enhance

  • use_gpus, devices

  • limit and dpi are accepted for compatibility and ignored

  • refreshed markdown/<stem>.md
  • refreshed cleaner/parquet metadata after OCR reruns
  • when metadata parquet is present, OCR now preserves the same row identity and embeds corrected text plus direct OCR sidecar pointers such as ocr_markdown_relpath, ocr_metrics_relpath, and ocr_text_sha256
  • json/<stem>.latex_map.jsonl when enrichment runs

docs.title: download()
docs.text:
download(
  input_parquet: str | Path | None = None,
  url_column: str = 'url',
  verbose: bool | None = None,
  *,
  parallelize_by: str | None = None,
  links_column: str | None = None,
  **kwargs,
) -> pd.DataFrame
  • Purpose: fetch source files described in a parquet dataset.
  • Typical inputs:
  • an explicit input_parquet
  • or the first parquet file found in input_dir
  • Important parameters:
  • links_column: override URL column name
  • parallelize_by: choose grouping for the scheduler
  • download_mode: one of standard, auto, or browser
  • browser_mode=True: alias for download_mode="browser"
  • download_policy_file: route specific domains/URL patterns to standard, auto, or browser
  • downloader kwargs via **kwargs for concurrency, SSL, retries, checkpoints, etc. Public targets only: a URL with userinfo or a credential query field, or a domain_cookies/credentials setting, is refused with credentials_unsupported before any request.
  • Main outputs:
  • downloaded files in downloads/
  • partial/final results in download_results/
  • returned pd.DataFrame with download status and metadata

Browser-capable download mode is intended for browser-gated file endpoints where a real file still exists behind session/bootstrap checks. It is not a general viewer extractor. Viewer-only sources should still fail cleanly with a recorded error and no local file artifact.

corpus.download(
    input_parquet="input_urls.parquet",
    download_mode="browser",
)

Policy-routed example:

corpus.download(
    input_parquet="input_urls.parquet",
    download_policy_file="download_policy.yml",
)

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
GlossAPI is a staged corpus-processing pipeline centered around the Corpus API.

Core extraction uses PDFium with Rust layout_v2 labels. Corpus.run() and the CLI execute a ledger-backed DAG with frozen settings and retention; individual phase methods retain compatibility filesystem/parquet behavior. Docling layout/math is optional, and OCR uses the pinned Greek toolkit.

GlossAPI therefore has two interfaces over the same stages:

  • Streaming runs (Corpus.run(), glossapi plan / glossapi run): one ledger-backed DAG recorded in corpus.sqlite3, with frozen settings, per-task attempts and retries, and retention of intermediates. See Resumability, Recovery, and Retention and Corpus-wide barriers.
  • Phase methods (download(), extract(), clean(), ocr(), section(), annotate(), jsonl(), jsonl_sharded()): individual calls that keep the compatibility behavior described below, where stages hand off through the output directory, filenames and the metadata parquet.

At a high level, the stages are:

  1. download()
  2. extract()
  3. clean()
  4. ocr()
  5. section()
  6. annotate()
  7. export: jsonl() / jsonl_sharded(), or the streaming export stage

Not every run uses every stage, but the stages are designed to compose through a shared output directory and shared metadata.

docs.title: Why the pipeline is staged
docs.text:
The staging is deliberate. Each stage exists because academic PDFs, especially Greek-language PDFs, fail in different ways:

  • downloads may fail, duplicate, or need retry logic
  • extraction may succeed structurally but produce unusable text
  • many Greek PDFs have broken or missing ToUnicode mappings
  • OCR is expensive, so it should be applied selectively
  • sectioning and annotation should operate only on documents considered usable
  • corpus analysis requires retaining what happened at each stage, not only the final text

The pipeline therefore separates:

  • acquisition
  • text extraction
  • text quality validation
  • remediation via OCR
  • structural segmentation
  • annotation
  • downstream export

docs.title: Main orchestration surface
docs.text:
The main user-facing object is Corpus in src/glossapi/corpus/corpus_orchestrator.py.

Corpus wires together phase mixins:

  • DownloadPhaseMixin
  • ExtractPhaseMixin
  • CleanPhaseMixin
  • OcrMathPhaseMixin
  • SectionPhaseMixin
  • AnnotatePhaseMixin
  • ExportPhaseMixin

This is the main organizational boundary in the codebase.

docs.title: 1. Download
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • fetch files from URL-bearing parquet inputs
  • preserve scraping metadata
  • produce local files plus download result metadata

Important characteristics:

  • async downloader
  • retry and rate-limit behavior
  • resume support from prior parquet results
  • filename normalization and collision avoidance

docs.title: 2. Extract
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • turn input documents into Markdown
  • with the optional Docling backend only, emit Docling JSON and formula index artifacts

Important characteristics:

  • the default safe backend uses PDFium and the bundled Rust extensions to write layout_v2 Markdown, with no Docling or GPU (GLOSSAPI_MARKDOWN_LAYOUT=plain selects plain page text)
  • the Docling backend is optional (the layout package); select it explicitly with phase1_backend='docling' when you need Docling layout JSON for math/code enrichment or Docling layout throughput
  • backend selection is part performance decision, part stability decision

docs.title: 3. Clean
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • clean Markdown
  • compute quality and badness metrics
  • identify documents that should be rerouted to OCR

Important characteristics:

  • uses Rust extension for speed and consistency
  • writes metrics back into metadata parquet
  • provides operational gating for downstream stages

docs.title: 4. OCR
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • OCR the physical pages that page quality routes, and optionally run math/code enrichment from existing Docling JSON

Important characteristics:

  • OCR uses the pinned Greek OCR toolkit (an optional install); retained native text is kept for pages that are not routed
  • reads metadata to find OCR candidates: by default (page_routing='all') routed pages in flagged and unflagged documents; page_routing='flagged' restricts OCR to cleaner-flagged documents
  • the phase method is skiplist-aware; a streaming run records task attempts and retries in the ledger instead
  • designed as a corrective stage, not the default for every document

docs.title: 5. Section
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • split Markdown documents into structural sections for classification and downstream analysis

Important characteristics:

  • prefers documents that passed quality checks or were repaired successfully
  • writes parquet section records

docs.title: 6. Annotate
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • classify sections with the packaged ML model
  • optionally produce fully annotated section outputs

docs.title: 7. Export
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • produce downstream JSONL- and parquet-friendly outputs
  • aggregate metadata from chunked and unchunked runs

docs.title: What makes GlossAPI operationally distinct
docs.text:
Four themes dominate the current design:

  1. Core extraction needs neither Docling nor a GPU; Docling is an optional backend for layout JSON, math/code enrichment and layout throughput.
  2. Optional backends (Docling, OCR) can be unstable under batching and parallelism, so recovery logic matters.
  3. Greek text validity is a first-class quality concern because raw extraction is often wrong even when it does not crash.
  4. Metadata is treated as a durable record of both original scraping context and pipeline-generated diagnostics.

Two more themes are equally important for maintainers:

  1. resumability and recovery semantics
  2. filesystem artifact and state contracts

docs.title: Typical run shape
docs.text:
For a practical corpus run, the intended flow is often:

  1. download the corpus
  2. extract to Markdown
  3. clean and score text quality
  4. OCR the pages page quality routes (in flagged and unflagged documents by default)
  5. section the resulting usable corpus
  6. optionally annotate and export

This allows expensive OCR to be focused on genuinely problematic files.

docs.title: Current architectural pressure points
docs.text:
The current architecture is effective but has important tradeoffs:

  • stage handoff depends partly on method calls and partly on filesystem conventions
  • the phase methods resume from file presence and metadata parquet state; a streaming run (Corpus.run(), glossapi run) resumes from the ledger corpus.sqlite3 instead
  • phase methods keep their intermediate artifacts, which improves auditing but increases storage; streaming runs apply the retention settings recorded in the ledger
  • filename-based identity is practical but puts pressure on future chunking and storage redesigns

These pressure points are documented separately in:

  • Artifact Layout and Stage Handoffs
  • OCR Cleaning Runtime
  • Resumability, Recovery, and Retention
  • Markdown Library Survey — design rationale for the parser-backed Phase A (Pilot B).

docs.title: Artifact Layout and Stage Handoffs
docs.text:
This document explains how the phase methods (extract(), clean(), ocr(), ...) use on-disk artifacts to pass work from one stage to the next. A streaming run (Corpus.run(), glossapi run) decides from the ledger corpus.sqlite3 and publishes these same directories at its corpus-wide barriers; see Resumability, Recovery, and Retention.

This is one of the most important implementation contracts in GlossAPI.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
The pipeline is not driven only by method calls. It is also driven by:

  • directories
  • filenames and stems
  • parquet metadata
  • presence or absence of stage artifacts

If these conventions change carelessly, stage chaining, reruns, and recovery can break.

docs.title: Core directories
docs.text:
The output directory typically contains these stage-relevant subdirectories:

  • downloads/: downloaded source files
  • download_results/: parquet metadata from acquisition and later updates
  • markdown/: extracted Markdown
  • clean_markdown/: cleaned Markdown
  • json/: Docling and metrics byproducts
  • sections/: section parquet outputs
  • logs/: logs and stage-specific operational traces

These are not arbitrary folders. They define the current stage handoff model.

docs.title: Download -> Extract
docs.text:
extract() expects source documents to be available through the corpus download layout, typically under downloads/.

This means the downloader is responsible for more than fetching bytes. It is also preparing the corpus for the extraction contract.

docs.title: Extract -> Clean
docs.text:
clean() operates on Markdown outputs from extraction, typically in markdown/.

This is the point where extracted text becomes quality-assessable data.

docs.title: Clean -> OCR
docs.text:
ocr() does not simply scan markdown files and OCR everything. It consults metadata, especially OCR-related flags and quality signals, to decide which documents require remediation.

This means the handoff is:

  • file artifacts from extraction
  • metadata judgments from cleaning

docs.title: Clean/OCR -> Section
docs.text:
section() should operate on documents considered usable, either because:

  • they passed quality checks
  • they were successfully repaired through OCR

So this handoff depends on both Markdown availability and stage metadata.

docs.title: Section -> Annotate / Export
docs.text: Later stages consume parquet outputs and related metadata rather than raw source files.

docs.title: Naming conventions
docs.text:
The pipeline uses filenames and normalized stems to reconnect outputs across directories.

This usually determines how the system finds relationships between:

  • source files
  • Markdown outputs
  • JSON outputs
  • metrics
  • chunked outputs
  • parquet metadata rows

This is practical, but it also means filenames act as part of document identity in the current design.

docs.title: Chunk-aware naming
docs.text:
Some processing modes produce chunked outputs, typically by encoding page ranges in filenames or stems.

That affects:

  • artifact discovery
  • metadata aggregation
  • export-time reconstruction

Chunk suffix behavior is therefore part of the current contract.

External OCR engines execute selected physical page ranges through Docling. The backend-neutral ocr/page_artifacts.py assembles canonical Markdown and metrics; downstream stages consume those canonical files and the updated metadata rows. Range artifacts are archived under sidecars/ocr_shards/; retained native Markdown and per-page replacements live under sidecars/ocr_native/ and sidecars/ocr_pages/. See OCR plugin migration.

docs.title: Authoritative state vs derived artifacts
docs.text:
Not every file has equal semantic importance.

The current system benefits from distinguishing:

  • authoritative metadata state
  • stage outputs needed downstream
  • optional or debug-oriented artifacts
  • rebuildable byproducts

This distinction becomes important for storage policy and future redesign.

docs.title: Operational risks in this model
docs.text:
The current on-disk contract is effective, but it creates risks:

  • directory scanning can encode hidden assumptions
  • filename-based identity can be fragile
  • chunk naming can become overloaded
  • retention of all intermediates can increase long-term storage costs

These are manageable as long as they are documented explicitly.

docs.title: Recommended contributor rule
docs.text:
If a change affects any of the following, treat it as a contract change and update docs:

  • directory names
  • file naming or stem normalization
  • chunk naming
  • which stage reads from which directory
  • which artifacts are required for rerun or downstream stages
  • where metadata parquet is expected to live

docs.title: Core Design Principles
docs.text: This document explains why the pipeline looks the way it does.

docs.title: 1. Throughput matters, but only if the run remains recoverable
docs.text:
GlossAPI uses Docling because it offers high-throughput extraction, rich layout handling, and integration paths for OCR and enrichment.

However, throughput is not pursued blindly. The pipeline is designed to retain progress and isolate problematic documents when instability appears.

Practical consequence:

  • batching and parallelism are useful
  • recovery and resumability are mandatory

docs.title: 2. Text extraction success is not the same as text quality success
docs.text:
A PDF can produce output without producing usable output.

This matters especially for Greek corpora because many files contain broken or absent ToUnicode mappings. As a result:

  • extraction may complete
  • Markdown may be non-empty
  • the text may still be unusable Greek

GlossAPI therefore treats text validation as a separate stage concern, not as an optional afterthought.

docs.title: 3. OCR is a corrective stage, not the default for every file
docs.text:
OCR is more expensive than text-layer extraction. Running OCR on everything would increase compute cost, runtime, and failure surface.

The pipeline instead tries to:

  1. extract cheaply where possible
  2. detect low-quality output
  3. reroute only bad files through OCR

This selective approach is central to the current design.

docs.title: 4. Metadata is a first-class product of the pipeline
docs.text:
The pipeline does not only produce Markdown. It also produces run metadata describing:

  • original acquisition context
  • extraction outcomes
  • quality metrics
  • OCR needs and OCR success
  • skip behavior
  • stage progression

This metadata is essential for:

  • resumability
  • debugging
  • corpus auditing
  • post-run data analysis

docs.title: 5. Filesystem structure is part of the contract
docs.text:
Stage outputs are not arbitrary temporary files. The pipeline expects specific folders, naming rules, and metadata locations.

That means contributors should treat:

  • artifact paths
  • naming conventions
  • parquet locations
  • chunk suffix behavior

as contract-like behavior unless deliberately redesigned.

docs.title: 6. Intermediate artifacts are retained intentionally (phase methods)
docs.text:
Individual phase methods keep their intermediate artifacts. A streaming run (Corpus.run(), glossapi run) instead applies the retention settings frozen in its ledger; see Resumability, Recovery, and Retention.

Keeping intermediate artifacts increases storage usage, but it provides strong benefits:

  • easier debugging
  • easier re-entry into later stages
  • auditability
  • ability to inspect what changed between stages

This is a deliberate tradeoff, not just accidental accumulation.

docs.title: 7. Recovery behavior is part of normal operation
docs.text:
The pipeline assumes that some documents will:

  • fail to download
  • fail to parse
  • time out
  • produce unusable Greek
  • crash Docling

So recovery is not a rare edge case. It is part of standard corpus processing.

docs.title: 8. Current implementation details should be distinguished from logical contracts
docs.text:
The phase methods rely heavily on:

  • filenames and stems
  • parquet files on local disk
  • retained intermediate artifacts

Streaming runs already implement the deeper contract in the ledger corpus.sqlite3 (document identities, task attempts, recorded inputs and outputs, retention). The logical contract is:

  • each document needs a stable identity
  • each stage needs explicit inputs and outputs
  • each stage should emit usable status and diagnostics
  • reruns should be able to distinguish success, failure, skip, and retry states

This distinction matters for future redesign work around storage, streaming, or chunk-level execution.

docs.title: Corpus-wide barriers of a streaming run
docs.text:
A streaming run (glossapi run, Corpus.run) processes each document through its stages as soon as its inputs exist. These are the only points where it waits for the whole corpus. plan --json previews exactly these rows for the planned stages (barriers, with executed_as, why and continues), and the run executes them as <stage>.compatibility_publish tasks, each chained after the previous one (corpus_seal dependencies), plus the source-manifest seal when the plan is frozen. tests/test_ledger_w18_barriers.py keeps the code, this table and the preview equal.

barrier brought by stage executed as why it waits what continues source_manifest always freeze The full requested source set and its expansion order fix download names and URL duplicates before any worker starts. Nothing runs before the seal; afterwards download, extract, clean and sections stream per document. download_publication download download.compatibility_publish download_results/ and downloads/ are written by the unchanged single-writer download serializer over the sealed manifest; it replays committed acquisitions and never fetches. Every document task (download, extract, clean, OCR, sections) runs before it; under memory_saving=extreme each owned download is already deleted after its last document reader. extract_publication extract extract.compatibility_publish markdown/, sidecars/extract/ and repaired_pdfs/ are published by the legacy extract wrapper, which replays committed extractions in one pass and merges per-document repair metadata once. Document extraction, cleaning, OCR and section parsing all finish before it; a download deleted under memory_saving=extreme is bound by its recorded hash and not read again. clean_publication clean clean.compatibility_publish clean_markdown/ and the cleaning report are written by the directory-level cleaner wrapper over the published raw markdown. Per-document cleaning already ran in the DAG; this publishes its committed outputs. ocr_publication ocr ocr.compatibility_publish OCR markdown is materialized and the cleaner refreshed over markdown/ by one publisher (OCR success metadata is a corpus parquet). Per-document OCR and its re-clean already ran in the DAG. sections_selection_ids sections sections.compatibility_publish Legacy section selection and global section IDs use corpus traversal order and the aggregate parquet needs the selected set. Per-document section parsing streams in the DAG; only selection, IDs and the aggregate parquet wait. annotation_batch annotate annotate.compatibility_publish Annotation predicts over PyArrow partitions, then materializes whole-corpus frames for post-processing and full annotation. Every document's sections are parsed before it; annotation itself does not stream yet. export_shards export export.compatibility_publish Ordered export membership and shard boundaries need the sealed selected set; every selected version gets an inclusion or omission receipt. Record preparation inputs are complete; the single publisher seals one generation.

Not barriers: - Durability: before any unlink a user or a later stage could need, the run makes the needed bytes and ledger rows durable with targeted fsyncs of the affected files and directories and a FULL ledger commit (K4(c) part 1; never syncfs). These are short waits inside a step, not corpus-wide waiting points. - Optional content-duplicate finalization is record-only today: it changes no membership and executes no barrier. - Directory-level cleaning, repair, routing, OCR and math kernels run per document inside the DAG; their directory wrappers appear above only as publications of committed results.

docs.title: Failure Recovery and Skiplist
docs.text:
One of the most important operational realities of GlossAPI is that Docling can fail in ways that matter at corpus scale.

This document describes the recovery model of the individual phase methods (extract(), ocr(), math enrichment). Docling is optional in 0.2.0: core extraction uses PDFium and Rust. A streaming run (Corpus.run(), glossapi run) records task attempts and retries in the ledger instead; see Resumability, Recovery, and Retention.

docs.title: Problem statement
docs.text:
Docling can provide excellent throughput, but under some conditions it may:

  • crash on specific PDFs
  • hang or time out
  • fail more often when batch size is greater than 1
  • make a worker or runner unusable after a bad document

At corpus scale, this is not a corner case. It is a design constraint.

docs.title: Recovery philosophy
docs.text:
GlossAPI does not assume every document is processable in a single clean pass.

Instead, the recovery model aims to:

  1. preserve successful work
  2. isolate problematic documents
  3. let the run continue where possible
  4. make the failure visible in retained metadata and artifacts
  5. avoid repeatedly crashing on the same bad inputs

docs.title: What the skiplist is for
docs.text:
The skiplist exists to record documents that should not be retried blindly during the same operational flow.

Its role is practical:

  • prevent repeated crashes on known-problematic files
  • preserve throughput for the rest of the corpus
  • make failure handling explicit rather than implicit

The skiplist is therefore part of the recovery system, not a convenience feature.

docs.title: Runner recovery
docs.text:
When the extraction or OCR path encounters problematic PDFs, the runner may need to:

  • discard the broken processing context
  • reinitialize the relevant engine
  • continue with the remaining documents

The important requirement is that recovery should preserve the ability to reason about the run afterward.

That means the pipeline should leave behind enough evidence to answer:

  • which file caused the problem
  • which stage failed
  • whether the document was skipped, timed out, or crashed the worker
  • whether the rest of the run continued successfully

docs.title: Relationship to batching
docs.text:
Batching is strongly connected to failure recovery.

With batch size greater than 1, one bad document can affect:

  • other documents in the same batch
  • the current worker state
  • the confidence that outputs from the current runner remain valid

That is why recovery semantics are just as important as batching semantics.

docs.title: Expected operator understanding
docs.text:
Operators should know:

  • skiplist use is not a silent corruption mechanism
  • skipped files are expected to be inspectable later
  • keeping the rest of the run alive is often better than insisting on full completion in one pass
  • repeated crashes on the same file should feed into the skiplist instead of consuming the whole run

docs.title: Expected contributor understanding
docs.text:
Contributors should know:

  • any new batching or concurrency logic must preserve recoverability
  • a failure on one file should not erase already successful outputs
  • stage metadata should remain analyzable after recovery
  • skip behavior should be explicit in metadata and logs

docs.title: Documentation checklist for this area
docs.text:
Any future change in this area should update docs if it affects:

  • skiplist file location
  • semantics of a skipped document
  • crash vs timeout classification
  • rerun behavior after recovery
  • whether a failed document can poison a worker or batch
  • which artifacts remain authoritative after a partial stage failure

docs.title: Long-term architectural note
docs.text:
The skiplist solves an operational problem in the current architecture. It should not be mistaken for the ideal long-term abstraction.

Long-term improvements may include:

  • more explicit per-document status records
  • better process isolation
  • chunk-aware scheduling
  • less dependence on filename-only identity

But in the current system, the skiplist is a key part of practical reliability.

docs.title: Docling Throughput and Batching
docs.text: Docling is the central extraction engine for GlossAPI when throughput, OCR integration, or richer layout processing is required.

docs.title: Why Docling is used
docs.text:
Docling provides several advantages that matter for this pipeline:

  • good extraction throughput
  • support for PDF layout processing
  • integration with OCR backends
  • support paths for formula and code enrichment
  • better fit for heterogeneous academic corpora than a purely minimal extractor

In GlossAPI, Docling is not just a library dependency. It is one of the main architectural choices.

docs.title: Backend model in GlossAPI
docs.text:
Phase 1 extraction distinguishes between:

  • a safer backend path
  • a Docling-oriented backend path

The backend is resolved in the extraction phase based on requested behavior. In practice:

  • safe extraction is preferred when no heavy OCR or enrichment path is required
  • Docling is selected when OCR or enrichment is needed
  • Docling may also be chosen when throughput is prioritized and the environment is stable enough

This is why the pipeline keeps both performance-oriented and defensive extraction behavior available.

docs.title: Batching and parallelism
docs.text:
The codebase is structured to support high-throughput extraction through:

  • batch policy configuration
  • thread configuration
  • accelerator selection
  • GPU-aware OCR integration when needed

Batching helps because setup overhead can dominate for small files, and corpora often contain many similar documents.

Parallelism helps because extraction is a corpus task, not usually a single-document task.

docs.title: Why batching is not a free win
docs.text:
In theory, increasing batch size should improve throughput. In practice, Docling can become unstable, especially with more than one file in flight under some configurations.

That means batching has to be understood as a controlled optimization, not as an unconditional default.

The operational question is not:

  • "Can Docling batch?"

It is:

  • "Can Docling batch in this environment, on this corpus, with recoverable failure semantics?"

docs.title: Throughput vs stability tradeoff
docs.text:
The project currently balances two goals:

  1. use Docling to get practical throughput
  2. isolate bad documents and preserve progress when Docling misbehaves

This is a key design tradeoff. Contributors should resist oversimplifying it in either direction:

  • purely maximizing batching can make runs fragile
  • purely disabling batching can make large corpora impractically slow

docs.title: What should be documented for operators
docs.text:
Operators need to understand:

  • which backend they are using
  • whether OCR or enrichment forces Docling behavior
  • whether batching is enabled
  • how to recognize when the throughput optimization is causing instability
  • what artifacts and metadata remain trustworthy after a partial failure

docs.title: What should be documented for contributors
docs.text:
Contributors need to understand:

  • where backend selection happens
  • where batch policy is configured
  • what assumptions exist around one-file vs multi-file processing
  • how failures should degrade
  • how output and metadata contracts must survive recovery

docs.title: Future design pressure
docs.text:
Docling throughput behavior is also connected to future architectural changes:

  • smaller storage footprint
  • chunk-level execution
  • lower operational fragility
  • clearer document identity beyond filename stems

For that reason, throughput policy should be documented as an operational strategy, not as an invisible implementation detail.

docs.title: Greek Text Validation
docs.text:
Greek text validation is a core quality gate in GlossAPI.

This is one of the most important parts of the pipeline because many Greek PDFs fail in ways that are not captured by simple extraction success.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text:
Many Greek PDFs have one or more of the following problems:

  • no ToUnicode mapping
  • broken ToUnicode mapping
  • incorrect text-layer encoding
  • text that is technically extractable but not semantically valid Greek

This means a document can produce Markdown that looks operationally successful while still being unusable.

docs.title: Why plain extraction success is insufficient
docs.text:
A successful file write does not prove:

  • the output is readable Greek
  • the output represents the original document correctly
  • the text layer is reliable enough to avoid OCR

This is why the pipeline separates:

  • extraction
  • quality validation
  • OCR remediation

docs.title: What the cleaner contributes
docs.text:
The cleaning stage uses Rust-backed metrics and heuristics to evaluate extracted text quality.

The cleaner does more than normalize Markdown. It also helps answer:

  • does this output look like valid Greek text?
  • is the output mostly Latin or mojibake?
  • is the document effectively empty after cleanup?
  • should this file be rerouted through OCR?

docs.title: Important metadata outcomes
docs.text:
Several metadata outputs are operationally important for Greek validation:

  • badness or quality scores
  • needs_ocr
  • filter classification
  • character-count-related diagnostics
  • OCR success after remediation

These fields are not just reporting detail. They determine downstream behavior.

docs.title: Why OCR is selective
docs.text:
For Greek corpora, OCR is necessary for many files but still should not be the default for every file.

Selective OCR is important because:

  • text-layer extraction is cheaper
  • many files do not need OCR
  • OCR introduces additional runtime and failure surface

So the current strategy is:

  1. extract normally
  2. validate text quality
  3. OCR only the files that look invalid or unreliable

docs.title: Common failure patterns in Greek corpora
docs.text:
Operators and contributors should expect issues such as:

  • consonant-heavy garbage output
  • mostly Latin text where Greek should exist
  • low-information or almost-empty Markdown
  • incorrect sigma or bigram patterns
  • severe mojibake

These are not niche anomalies. They are part of the expected workload.

docs.title: Why this should be documented prominently
docs.text:
Without this context, a new contributor may assume:

  • extraction already solved the problem
  • OCR is optional polish
  • quality validation is just cleanup

All three assumptions would be wrong for the target corpus.

Greek validation is one of the main reasons the pipeline exists in this form.

docs.title: Operator guidance
docs.text:
When evaluating a run, operators should be able to answer:

  • which files passed extraction but failed Greek quality checks
  • which files were marked needs_ocr
  • which files improved after OCR
  • which files remain problematic even after OCR

docs.title: Contributor guidance
docs.text:
Any change to extraction, cleaning, OCR routing, or scoring should be evaluated against this question:

  • does this make the pipeline better or worse at distinguishing valid Greek from technically successful but unusable output?

If that question is not addressed, the change is incomplete.

docs.title: Markdown Library Survey
docs.text:
Contributor design history

This page records the design rationale behind the cleaner's parser-backed Phase A. It is background for contributors, not installation or runtime guidance for GlossAPI 0.2.0.

This document captures the design rationale behind the cleaner's parser-backed Phase A. It surveys established Markdown parsers, formatters, and renderers across Rust, C, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Go, and Pandoc/Haskell, then maps the lessons onto the choices that landed in the production cleaner.

The goal was never to replace the cleaner with one of these tools wholesale. The goal was to extract design lessons for Docling-produced Markdown corpus cleanup: make raw Markdown closer to rendered preview while preserving the rendered element graph.

The conclusions of this survey shipped as Pilot B — the parser-backed format_surgical_checked path that is now the production Phase A. See OCR Cleaning Runtime for the runtime architecture that consumes this layer, and rust/glossapi_rs_cleaner/src/md_format_surgical.rs for the implementation.

docs.title: Sources consulted
docs.text:
• Comrak and comrak docs.rs
  • pulldown-cmark guide
  • cmark-gfm
  • remark
  • markdown-it
  • mdformat
  • Prettier options
  • goldmark
  • Pandoc manual
  • GitHub Flavored Markdown spec

docs.title: Executive takeaways
docs.text:
The main ecosystem lesson: do not hand-roll Markdown grammar with regexes when correctness matters. Mature projects either parse Markdown into an AST or event stream and then transform/serialize, or they make formatting choices explicit and configurable.

The original line-based cleaner moved in the right direction with pulldown-cmark verification, but the transforms themselves still relied on line heuristics — that is exactly where the highest-risk findings in the implementation review came from.

Direction adopted (status as of the cleaner integration):

  1. ✅ Rust remained the production implementation language.
  2. ✅ A parser-backed Markdown normalization path landed using comrak (Pilot B / md_format_surgical).
  3. ✅ pulldown-cmark is kept as the fast independent verifier in dual_verify, not as the formatter.
  4. ✅ cmark-gfm/Pandoc/mdformat are treated as differential oracles in sampled tests, not hot-path dependencies. cmark-gfm is the dev-only ground-truth oracle when installed; production uses dual_verify (comrak + pulldown-cmark) only.
  5. ✅ Raw-readability is explicit: the corpus default unwraps soft-wrapped prose while preserving hard breaks (Pilot B's three target transforms — paragraph reflow, GFM separator minimization, HR canonicalization).

docs.title: Rust: pulldown-cmark
docs.text:
What it offers:

  • Pull-parser event stream for CommonMark with GFM-style options such as tables, task lists, strikethrough, footnotes, admonitions, and math.
  • Low memory, high performance, and a good fit for verification because it can render HTML from events.
  • The guide highlights pull parsing and notes that consecutive text events can occur, with TextMergeStream available to smooth text iteration.

What we learned:

  • Use it for strict/structural verification, especially as an independent parser from any future formatter.
  • Use its Event::SoftBreak and Event::HardBreak semantics as a model for reflow: only rewrite soft breaks, never hard breaks.
  • Avoid building production formatting around HTML output alone; event streams are excellent for checking, but source-preserving rewriting needs either source spans or an AST renderer.

docs.title: Rust: comrak
docs.text:
What it offers:

  • CommonMark and GFM-compatible parser/renderer in Rust.
  • Parses to an AST, allows AST manipulation, and supports format_commonmark / markdown_to_commonmark.
  • Fine-grained parse/render options and custom formatter support to override rendering of node types.

What we learned:

  • This was the best Rust candidate for a parser-backed Phase A. Pilot B uses comrak's AST + sourcepos to walk top-level block children and render only Paragraph/Table/ThematicBreak nodes, copying everything else verbatim from source.
  • Full reserialization (the abandoned Pilot A approach) over-normalized list markers, link forms, escapes, and other syntax. The surgical approach — re-render only the three target node types — was needed to avoid those side effects.

docs.title: C: cmark-gfm
docs.text:
What it offers:

  • GitHub's fork of the C CommonMark reference implementation, with GFM extensions.
  • Parses to an AST, supports AST manipulation, and renders to HTML, CommonMark, XML, LaTeX, groff man, and more.
  • Conformance, speed, fuzzing, and standardized behavior.

What we learned:

  • Use cmark-gfm as a differential oracle when installed (development hosts only).
  • Its XML AST output is useful for golden fixtures.
  • Do not bind it into production. C FFI is extra operational surface area; comrak is already Rust-native and sufficient for dual_verify.

docs.title: JavaScript/TypeScript: remark / unified
docs.text:
What it offers:

  • Unified processor that parses Markdown and serializes Markdown using remark-parse and remark-stringify.
  • Uses mdast as the syntax tree.
  • Lint plugins and configurable stringify settings for stylistic rules such as ordered-list markers and setext/ATX heading choices.

What we learned:

  • Separate "parse", "transform", "lint", and "stringify" as distinct phases. That maps cleanly onto the Phase A / Phase B / verification split.
  • Add lint-like diagnostics to the scorecard, not only pass/fail verification.
  • Markdown dialect handling should be modular, not encoded as ad hoc checks scattered across the cleaner.

docs.title: JavaScript: markdown-it
docs.text:
What it offers:

  • CommonMark-oriented parser with GFM tables/strikethrough, plugin rules, and configurable syntax.
  • CommonMark support, extensibility, high speed, and safe rendering defaults.

What we learned:

  • Treat dialect features as enabled rule sets. There should be a clear MarkdownDialect::GfmDocling profile instead of assuming every pipe-like line means one thing.
  • Safety defaults matter. For us that means "do not normalize unknown syntax unless the parser confirms it is a known Markdown element."

docs.title: Python: mdformat
docs.text:
What it offers:

  • CommonMark-compliant Markdown formatter, CLI and Python library.
  • Opinionated style: consistent indentation/whitespace, ATX headings, sorted link references, fenced code instead of indented code, 1. ordered-list markers.
  • Intentionally does not change word wrapping by default to support semantic line breaks.
  • Plugins for additional Markdown engines/dialects; escapes engine-specific syntax when it cannot safely understand it.

What we learned:

  • Full-document formatters make many style decisions outside our scope. We should not blindly run mdformat over corpus rows.
  • The plugin/dialect model is valuable. Unknown dialect syntax should be either preserved or escaped/diagnosed, not "cleaned" by regex.
  • Default wrapping caution is relevant, but our objective differs: Docling line breaks are usually layout artifacts, not semantic line breaks. The policy is now explicit (see §Executive takeaways item 5).

docs.title: Prettier Markdown
docs.text:
What it offers:

  • A proseWrap option with modes: always, never, and preserve.
  • Default is preserve because some services have linebreak-sensitive renderers, but never intentionally unwraps prose blocks into single lines.

What we learned:

  • The cleaner's corpus default is the equivalent of Prettier's never for prose paragraphs (Docling layout-induced soft breaks are unwrapped).
  • Verification enforces that unwrap only rewrites parser-observed soft breaks, not hard breaks, code, HTML-sensitive blocks, tables, or line-block-like content.

docs.title: Go: goldmark
docs.text:
What it offers:

  • CommonMark-compliant Go parser with AST, source positions, parser transformers, AST transformers, and renderers.
  • Built-in GFM extension bundle.
  • Extension APIs include block parsers, inline parsers, paragraph transformers, AST transformers, and renderers.

What we learned:

  • Source positions are the missing primitive that comrak's sourcepos: true provides — it is what lets Pilot B map AST nodes back to byte ranges and rewrite only the paragraph/table/HR spans we intend to touch.
  • Paragraph transformers are a strong pattern for the reflow pass: normalize paragraph text after block parsing, before final rendering.
  • The architecture reinforces the need to separate block parsing from inline parsing.

docs.title: Pandoc
docs.text:
What it offers:

  • Many Markdown variants and writer options.
  • --wrap=auto|none|preserve controls source-level output wrapping.
  • The Markdown philosophy that plain text should be readable; ordinary paragraph newlines are treated as spaces, while two trailing spaces or backslash create hard line breaks.

What we learned:

  • Pandoc's --wrap=none is the closest existing user-facing behavior to the desired raw corpus mode.
  • Pandoc is a good differential oracle for small samples but is too heavyweight for the hot path.

docs.title: 1. Parser-backed Phase A — ✅ landed as Pilot B
docs.text:
Implemented in rust/glossapi_rs_cleaner/src/md_format_surgical.rs:

input markdown
  → parse with comrak (GFM options + sourcepos)
  → walk top-level block children
  → re-render Paragraph / Table / ThematicBreak nodes
  → copy everything else verbatim from source
  → verify with dual_verify (comrak + pulldown-cmark HTML agreement on input + output)
  → on disagreement: ship input verbatim; record fallback_reason

The three target transformations:

  • Thematic break canonicalization — render parser-confirmed ThematicBreak as ---.
  • Table delimiter canonicalization — render parser-confirmed table delimiter cells as ---, :---, ---:, or :---:.
  • Paragraph softbreak unwrap — serialize parser-confirmed paragraph soft breaks as spaces, while preserving hard breaks.

docs.title: 2. Line-based path — ✅ removed entirely
docs.text: The original "fast line-based path as conservative fallback" recommendation was reconsidered: with dual_verify providing per-doc safety, the line-based path's value as fallback was eclipsed by Pilot B's verbatim-on-disagreement behavior. The line-based code (md_module::normalize_md_syntax) was removed in the cleaner integration.

docs.title: 3. Multi-parser verification oracles — ✅ landed as dual_verify
docs.text: Production cleaning runs dual_verify(input, output) on every Pilot B rewrite — comrak + pulldown-cmark HTML agreement. cmark-gfm is consulted when present (development hosts) as the ground-truth oracle.

docs.title: 4. Explicit dialect and formatting policy — ✅ landed as PhaseAPolicy
docs.text: md_format_surgical::PhaseAPolicy carries the active dialect choices (comrak/cmark-gfm autolink behavior, hard-break preservation, softbreak whitespace trim policy). Surfaced through PyO3 as phase_a_policy_py so callers and scorecards can log what was in effect.

docs.title: 5. AST-preserving transformations as the strongest invariant — ✅ landed
docs.text: The dual_verify check enforces preview-preservation under both parsers. When either parser sees the input rendering differently from the output, the rewrite is refused and input is shipped verbatim. The phase_a_fallback_reason field surfaces the cause for downstream sampling.

docs.title: Still open
docs.text: These directions from the survey have NOT yet landed. They remain reasonable next steps if the cleaner's correctness or coverage is extended further.

docs.title: Pseudo-table unwrapping as a separate semantic transform
docs.text: The ecosystem tools preserve tables because they are valid Markdown structures. If the corpus needs TOC pseudo-tables converted to prose, that is not formatting — it is a semantic structural rewrite. It needs its own module, its own classifier, a distinct invariant (table-to-list/prose mapping with preserved cell text order), and separate scorecard metrics. Do not mix pseudo-table unwrapping into Phase A.

docs.title: Raw-readability scorecard metrics beyond CleanStats
docs.text: CleanStats already tracks per-rule counts and per-doc 4-way char accounting. The survey suggested extra readability-oriented metrics (softbreaks_before/after, mean_physical_lines_per_paragraph_before/after, hr_run_width_before/after, etc.) that would give a more direct answer to "did raw Markdown become closer to rendered Markdown?". These are not in the current CleanStats schema.

docs.title: Lint-style diagnostic categories
docs.text: Pass/fail verification (dual_verify agreement) is in production. Per-category lint diagnostics (hard_break_preserved, softbreak_unwrapped, table_delimiter_minimized, etc.) would help when investigating regressions but are not implemented today.
