docs.title: Metadata, Artifacts, and Run Diagnostics
docs.text:
GlossAPI preserves both source metadata and pipeline-generated metadata.

This is a central feature of the system, not a side effect.

docs.title: Two kinds of metadata
docs.text:
The pipeline needs to retain:

  1. original metadata from scraping or source discovery
  2. pipeline metadata generated during processing

Original metadata helps preserve context such as:

  • source URL
  • filename assignment context
  • source collection information
  • document type or source-specific attributes

Pipeline metadata helps answer:

  • what happened to this document during processing
  • which stages ran
  • what quality issues were detected
  • whether the document was skipped, failed, repaired, or exported

docs.title: Why both matter
docs.text:
Without source metadata, the corpus loses provenance.

Without pipeline metadata, the run becomes difficult to debug or analyze.

GlossAPI needs both because it is not only extracting text. It is curating a processing history.

docs.title: Metadata as the state backbone
docs.text:
The metadata parquet is a key state object in the current architecture.

It is used to:

  • preserve prior results across reruns
  • select OCR candidates
  • track processing stage progression
  • join source context with derived quality information
  • support post-run analytics

This is why metadata updates should be treated carefully and documented whenever field semantics change.

In a streaming run (Corpus.run(), glossapi run) the authority is the ledger corpus.sqlite3; the metadata parquet (download_results/download_results.parquet) is a compatibility table the run publishes for the phase methods and for callers that read it. The rules below apply to that table.

docs.title: Rows without a file name
docs.text: A skipped duplicate URL and a failed download have an empty filename. Metadata merges never key such rows by file name: each one is kept as its own row, with its own URL, error and source fields. When the download results are folded into an existing download_results.parquet, a row without a file name replaces the canonical row without a file name that records the same URL, or is added. A file name that appears on several rows receives the artifact evidence (extraction, metrics) on each of them.

docs.title: Column types
docs.text: Metadata unions keep every value exactly. Integer columns stay integers when rows are added (values above 2**53 are never rounded); a column becomes the nullable Int64 (or UInt64) type only when a float could not hold its values. A union that would turn a categorical, a time-zone-aware datetime, a period or an interval column into plain objects is refused with MetadataSchemaError before anything is written; two categoricals with different categories are merged into one categorical. Decimal and list values are stored as the parquet serializer stores them (objects); their exact Python type is not guaranteed on read.

docs.title: Which metadata parquet each phase reads
docs.text: Two read rules exist. Corpus.clean looks first for a metadata parquet in input_dir, then ensures output_dir/download_results/download_results.parquet, then one in input_dir. Corpus.section, Corpus.ocr and math enrichment ensure the output's canonical table first, then search output_dir, then input_dir and input_dir/download_results. A Corpus object remembers the first parquet it resolved (or the metadata_path given to its constructor), and every later phase of that object uses it. When input_dir contains its own metadata parquet, call the phases on one Corpus object, or pass metadata_path, so that every phase uses the same file.

docs.title: Math enrichment flags
docs.text: enriched_math / math_enriched in the metadata parquet is a compatibility projection: it is true once math enrichment ran for the document, including a run that found no formula (math_items = 0). It does not distinguish an empty result from a failure; glossapi status and glossapi report (the ledger) do.

docs.title: Diagnostic information that should survive the run
docs.text:
A good corpus run should leave enough metadata and artifacts to analyze:

  • downloads that succeeded or failed
  • extraction outputs that were produced
  • files marked as low quality
  • files rerouted through OCR
  • files skipped because of known issues
  • files that reached sectioning or annotation

This supports both debugging and corpus-quality assessment.

docs.title: Blockers, issues, and post-run analysis
docs.text:
One of the design goals of the pipeline is to recognize blockers and stage issues for later analysis.

That means the system should make it possible to distinguish:

  • success
  • recoverable failure
  • skip
  • timeout
  • quality failure
  • rerun candidate
  • downstream blocker

If these states become ambiguous, post-run analysis quality drops sharply.

docs.title: Artifacts as evidence
docs.text:
Retained artifacts matter because they are often the easiest way to inspect what happened:

  • raw downloaded files
  • extracted Markdown
  • cleaned Markdown
  • Docling JSON
  • metrics JSON
  • section parquet outputs
  • logs

These artifacts complement metadata rather than replacing it.

docs.title: Documentation guidance
docs.text:
Each stage should document:

  • which metadata it reads
  • which metadata it writes
  • which artifacts it creates
  • which statuses or issue classes it can introduce

This makes it possible to reason about the run as a whole instead of as isolated methods.

docs.title: Long-term design note
docs.text:
The current design mixes:

  • metadata as durable logical state
  • artifacts as operational evidence
  • some filesystem-based inference

That works well today, but it is also a useful place to identify future refactoring opportunities:

  • more explicit document identity
  • clearer status schemas
  • better retention classes for artifacts
  • less inference from directory scanning alone

docs.title: OCR Cleaning Runtime
docs.text: This document explains how the current OCR cleaner is organized, why the matcher families are separated, and why the clean/debug behavior is driven by one shared page analyzer.

docs.title: One Analyzer, Two Render Modes
docs.text:
The OCR cleaner now works in two modes over the same span plan:

  • debug
  • preserves the source page surface
  • inserts <match ...> tags around the matched regions
  • clean
  • applies the removal/rewrite policy directly
  • writes the cleaned page text with no debug tags

This is deliberate. The project previously had a tendency for the reviewer-facing debug logic to evolve faster than the real cleaner. Sharing one analyzer avoids that drift: if the debug page is right, the clean page is operating on the same decisions.

The same alignment rule applies to metadata. When clean_ocr() writes cleaned markdown, it now scores parquet-facing OCR metrics from that cleaned directory. Without that, downstream export can read cleaned text while still carrying raw-OCR char_count_no_comments, is_empty, or repeat diagnostics in parquet.

docs.title: Code Layout
docs.text:
The OCR cleaner is split by responsibility so detector policy does not drift into rendering or table-specific cleanup:

  • src/glossapi/corpus/phase_clean.py
  • owns analyzer order, worker orchestration, and clean/debug mode selection
  • src/glossapi/corpus/ocr_table.py
  • owns HTML-table classification, dropping policy, and HTML->Markdown conversion
  • src/glossapi/corpus/ocr_render.py
  • owns span merging, clean/debug rendering, and match_index.jsonl row generation
  • src/glossapi/corpus/text_surface_metrics.py
  • owns shared published-surface metric helpers such as char_count_no_comments and is_empty

This split is deliberate. The project needs one place to decide what a match is, and a separate place to decide how that decision becomes visible output. That boundary is one of the main protections against random debug/clean drift.

docs.title: Stage Boundary: clean_ocr() vs clean()
docs.text:
These two stages deliberately remain separate:

  • clean_ocr()
  • sits on the corpus.ocr path
  • owns OCR artifact removal and OCR-specific metrics
  • clean()
  • sits primarily on the corpus.extract path
  • owns broader clean/export quality metrics

The OCR rerun path reuses clean() afterward because export still expects the generic clean/export fields. That reuse is intentional orchestration, not an argument that the two stages should collapse into one function.

docs.title: Field Ownership
docs.text:
The practical parquet contract is:

  • OCR-owned fields
  • percentage_greek
  • latin_percentage
  • polytonic_ratio
  • char_count_no_comments
  • is_empty
  • ocr_noise_suspect
  • ocr_noise_flags
  • ocr_repeat_phrase_run_max
  • ocr_repeat_line_run_max
  • ocr_repeat_suspicious_line_count
  • ocr_repeat_suspicious_line_ratio
  • clean/export-owned fields
  • greek_badness_score
  • mojibake_badness_score
  • needs_ocr
  • filter
  • other generic quality-routing fields

This ownership split is the reason the post-OCR sequence is explicit:

  1. clean_ocr() updates the OCR-owned layer on the OCR-cleaned text surface.
  2. clean(..., write_cleaned_files=False) refreshes the generic clean/export layer on that same surface.

docs.title: Why The Cleaner Is Not One Generic Matcher
docs.text:
The cleaner is trying to remove OCR- or VLM-induced garbage, not every repeated pattern in a page. A single fuzzy matcher over the whole page overgeneralizes quickly:

  • numbers steal matches that should belong to numeric progression logic
  • repeated notation in LaTeX looks like corruption even when it is legitimate
  • HTML tables distort text surfaces and cause spurious word matches

So the runtime uses ownership by surface type and structure instead of one broad "repetition" rule.

docs.title: Page Ownership Order
docs.text:
The current analyzer order is:

  1. tables
  2. numeric
  3. LaTeX
  4. hybrid numbered repetition
  5. shared text repetition

Why this order:

  • Tables run first because HTML table shells can dominate a page and confuse every later pass.
  • Numeric runs before generic text because 1, 2, 3, ... style progressions are real OCR-collapse signals and should not be absorbed by word_repeat.
  • LaTeX and hybrid passes run before generic text because they depend on local structure, not just repeated tokens.
  • Shared text repetition runs last on the remaining visible surface only.

This ordering is the main false-positive control mechanism.

docs.title: Table Cleaning Is Broader Than Repetition
docs.text:
Table handling is intentionally separated into src/glossapi/corpus/ocr_table.py because it is not just another repetition matcher.

Current table classes:

  • sentence_shell_table
  • a table with one prose-like filled cell
  • treated as layout noise around content
  • dropped in clean mode
  • empty_table_collapse
  • a large sparse shell with almost no real cell content
  • dropped in clean mode
  • repeated_rows
  • an actually repetition-oriented table problem
  • dropped in clean mode
  • unmatched kept tables
  • converted from HTML to GitHub-style Markdown

The important design point is that sentence-shell and empty-shell tables are structural cleanup decisions, not repetition decisions.

docs.title: LaTeX And Hybrid Generalization Strategy
docs.text:
LaTeX and hybrid numbered matching both follow the same conservative pattern:

  • prefer local runs
  • abstract slot fields
  • require mechanical progression or stable low-diversity cycles
  • avoid page-wide reuse as evidence on its own

That is why the cleaner does not treat "same symbol appears many times on a page" as enough evidence. The goal is to catch degenerate local collapse, not normal scholarly notation reuse.

docs.title: Why Rust Is Used Selectively
docs.text:
The hot-path detection work is in Rust because page-scale scanning dominates run time. Python still owns:

  • orchestration
  • filesystem I/O
  • debug/clean rendering
  • policy composition across matcher families

This split is intentional:

  • Rust is best for large repeated scans and token-normalization hot loops
  • Python is still easier for mode-aware rendering and pipeline integration

docs.title: Performance And Correctness Contract
docs.text:
Performance work is allowed only if exact debug output stays stable.

The correctness lock is:

  • tests/test_ocr_golden_pages.py

That suite uses hundreds of real pages and compares exact output bytes. The speed work therefore optimizes implementation, not semantics. The real-page fixture is external and owner-supplied (it is not distributed with the repository): set GLOSSAPI_OCR_GOLDEN_DIR to its root to run the suite; without it the test skips with that reason.

docs.title: Resumability, Recovery, and Retention
docs.text:
GlossAPI is designed to process corpora that are too large and too messy to assume a perfect one-pass run. This page describes how a run resumes, how it recovers from failures, and what it keeps on disk.

There are two ways to run the pipeline:

  • A streaming run: glossapi run or Corpus.run(). Every stage attempt is recorded in the corpus ledger corpus.sqlite3, and resume, retry, retention, glossapi status and glossapi report decide from that ledger.
  • The phase methods called one by one (Corpus.extract(), Corpus.clean(), ...). They resume from the metadata parquet and the files on disk, as before the ledger existed (see "Phase methods" below).

docs.title: Stage profiles
docs.text: The default stage profile (cutover) writes the provenance ledger (corpus.sqlite3) and decides from it: plan, run, resume, retention and status/report. GLOSSAPI_STAGE_PROFILE=legacy runs the pre-ledger stage code as a comparison control; its wrappers only record observations. sequential-adapters is the earlier qualification profile (CPU, one device, no batching, no OCR plugin).

docs.title: Resuming a run
docs.text:
• glossapi run --corpus CORPUS --resume RUN_ID (or Corpus.run(resume=RUN_ID)) restores the run's frozen plan and settings. Any other planning argument is refused (invalid_request).
  • A completed run is not executed again: resume checks the frozen execution environment and the retained recovery files by size and SHA-256, and returns the saved result.
  • Interrupted or lost attempts (attempt_interrupted, worker_lost, worker_process_crashed, extract_timeout) are retried automatically, within the run and on resume, at most 3 attempts per task. Every interrupted attempt counts, so a task whose worker is killed three times stays failed.
  • Other failures, and tasks past that budget, stay failed. glossapi run --resume RUN_ID --retry-failed is the explicit, operator-authorised retry of the failed tasks of that run.
  • A corpus publication (raw and cleaned markdown, sections, annotation, export) records which document versions it covers. It is current only while that set equals the documents that are now complete: when a retry brings failed documents to ok, every publication is repeated, so clean_markdown/, export.jsonl and the census include them. A resume without --retry-failed changes nothing and republishes nothing. A run that ends with failed documents keeps its other documents' private stage products until a later resume completes, because a repeated publication is made from them. If one is gone anyway and the work cannot be repeated (its own input, for example a download retired under memory_saving=extreme, was released), the resume refuses with republish_inputs_released (exit 2) before it repeats or publishes anything; start a new run over those sources. A vanished product whose input is still there is simply produced again. An amended plan is a new run with its own publications.
  • A stage worker that misses its deadline is stopped together with its descendants before its replacement starts. On Linux this includes descendants that moved to another process group (found through /proc). On macOS only the worker's own process group is signalled, so a descendant that detached into its own group (for example a browser) is not fenced there.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: One failed document does not stop the others. glossapi status lists each task's state and exits 1 when a listed task failed, with one typed error per failed task. glossapi report is the census (every requested source exactly once: produced, excluded, unavailable, failed or pending), and glossapi report --why DOCUMENT explains one document from the ledger alone, also after its intermediates were released.

docs.title: Retention: what a run keeps
docs.text:
Two settings, fixed when the run starts:

setting contract debug=off (default) An intermediate is released only after every planned reader has succeeded on its exact hash. Supplied files, selected final products, evidence and the ledger are kept. debug=on Keep every stage's intermediates and attempts, including bounded inner HTTP request bodies. memory_saving=normal (default) Never delete a supplied original or a downloaded file. memory_saving=extreme Delete only downloads this run owns, after the last planned reader succeeds and outputs are durable. Never a supplied original, another run's file, or a path reached through a link. Requires a disk budget.
  • Private scratch (under .glossapi/artifacts/) is released in groups: one summary per stage records the released files, their hashes and the planned readers. With debug=off the per-file release steps of private scratch are not kept in the ledger; producer hashes, every stage outcome, every deletion of a user-visible or source file and the run summary are.
  • The cleaned texts (clean_markdown/) and the per-document extraction sidecars (sidecars/extract/) are kept in every setting.

docs.title: Durability
docs.text:
• The ledger runs in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL: an ordinary commit survives the death of the process (SIGKILL), not a power loss.
  • Before every unlink that a user or a later stage could need, and at run close, the run makes exactly the needed bytes durable: it fsyncs the affected files, then their parent directories inside the corpus, then commits the ledger with synchronous=FULL. It never calls syncfs.
  • Policy deletions run in batches of up to 128 files. Each batch records its intents, unlinks the files, fsyncs every affected parent directory once, and only then commits the deletion records. A crash in between leaves recoverable intents; the next start finishes or re-checks them. Private scratch released inside a run is not made durable at all: after a crash its release is recovered and the stage runs again from kept inputs.
  • Corpus copies the run close leaves unflushed (for example export.jsonl and the metadata parquets, whose managed source is durable) are verified at the next start. A copy whose bytes no longer match is restored from its managed source only when its bytes are what a power loss can leave: a torn image of the managed bytes (a prefix, or blocks that read as zeros) or the copy this ledger registered there before. Timestamps never prove a copy unchanged. Any other content is treated as your edit: it is kept, and every start refuses (PostCloseEditError, typed code post_close_edit; the CLI reports it with that code, details.paths, and exit 3) until you move or delete it, after which it is republished from the managed source. Between a run close and the next start, a reader of such a copy can see a torn file after a power loss.

Declared residuals: an edit that only truncates a copy to a prefix of the managed bytes, within the same clock tick as the run close, is indistinguishable from a torn copy and is restored. Two process caches compare file identity (device, inode, size, mtime, ctime) and can miss a same-size rewrite that keeps mtime and ctime within one clock tick: the ledger's integrity trust and the registry of glossAPI's own file hashes. Destructive steps re-read the bytes they rely on. The original-hash cache keeps an original only when its mtime and ctime were already more than one second old when it was read, so a later write always invalidates it.

docs.title: memory_saving=extreme setup
docs.text:
memory_saving=extreme needs positive disk_budget_bytes, max_source_bytes and max_attempt_bytes (disk_budget_required otherwise). The guard reads the filesystems and never mounts anything. It requires:

  • Linux;
  • the corpus folder and CORPUS/.glossapi/staging each to be a mount point of its own size-limited filesystem, on different devices;
  • the two capacities together to be at most disk_budget_bytes, and the staging capacity at most max_attempt_bytes;
  • the corpus capacity to hold one attempt reservation (2 × max_attempt_bytes) plus the emergency reserve (max(1 GiB, 5% of the budget) + 64 MiB).

Anything else, including an ordinary shared volume, is refused with disk_guard_unavailable (exit 3). Admission then runs one attempt at a time.

Before the first publication, and again before each publication, the run checks that the corpus filesystem has room for what the remaining publications add: their input snapshots, products, the export's generation and published copy, re-published metadata tables and parquet footprints, minus the private scratch the run releases between publications (only files fully released, after their last reader, and nothing while a document of the run is failed, because those releases then do not happen). After the clean publication only the documents selected for sections are charged to sections and annotation. Measured on a 242-PDF cohort, the charge was 1.01–1.12× the real need at every check made after the selection is known and 1.04–1.08× for document-export-only runs; before the selection exists, the sections and annotation charge counts every document (7.2× there). A run that does not fit is refused with disk_budget_exceeded. If a publication still fills the disk, the run stops with a typed disk_full error, an interruption record, and can be resumed.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Linked products after a killed debug-off run. If a debug=off run is killed before its private release, the corpus products may still be hard links to the run's private copies until the next run closes. Running a legacy-profile writer (GLOSSAPI_STAGE_PROFILE=legacy) on such a corpus in that window can write through a link into the private copy. The default profile is not affected: it publishes by copying and replaces a linked destination first. Resume or close the killed run before using the legacy profile on the same corpus.
  • Annotation memory. Annotation (Corpus.annotate, and the annotate publication of glossapi run) reads the whole classified output back into memory twice: the classifier's prediction parts are concatenated into one frame for the index/threshold post-processing, and the full-annotation step reads classified_sections.parquet whole. Memory therefore grows with the total section text of the corpus. Measured on a 242-PDF cohort (409 sections, a 53.2 MB sections_for_annotation.parquet): peak RSS 983 MB (125 MB when the call started, +859 MB, 5.4 s); each whole read turns about 52.6 MB of parquet into a 122.7 MB frame. The measured total peak (983,224,320 bytes) is 18.49 times the sections parquet (53,185,990 bytes); the increase over the start of the call (858,636,288 bytes) is 16.14 times it. Projection, not measured beyond that cohort: assuming the increase grows linearly with the parquet on top of a fixed starting footprint of about 125 MB, a corpus with a 1 GB sections parquet needs about 16.3 GB at peak.

docs.title: Phase methods
docs.text:
Called one by one, the phase methods resume from the metadata parquet (download_results/download_results.parquet) and the files on disk: extraction skips files the parquet records as processed (skip_existing=True), and the download skips URLs that already succeeded. No pickle state file is written or read. They keep everything they write:

  • source files, intermediate Markdown, cleaned Markdown, Docling JSON and metrics JSON;
  • section and annotation parquets;
  • problematic_files/ and timeout_files/ from extraction, and logs.

Retention deletes nothing outside a streaming run.

docs.title: Stage Reference
docs.text:
This section documents the current contract of each major pipeline stage.

Each stage page covers:

  • purpose
  • main inputs
  • main outputs
  • key metadata interactions
  • failure and recovery concerns

Stage order:

  1. Download
  2. Extract
  3. Clean
  4. OCR
  5. Section
  6. Annotate
  7. Export

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The annotate stage classifies extracted sections and optionally produces more complete annotation outputs.

docs.title: Main responsibilities
docs.text:
• load section parquet outputs
  • apply the packaged section-classifier model
  • optionally perform fuller annotation behavior
  • preserve document-type context when available

docs.title: Main inputs
docs.text:
• section parquet outputs
  • classifier model
  • optional document-type metadata

docs.title: Main outputs
docs.text:
• classified section parquet
  • fully annotated section parquet when enabled

docs.title: Dependency note
docs.text: This stage depends on model availability. If the model is missing, the stage should fail clearly or skip clearly rather than silently pretending annotation succeeded.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Annotation reads the whole classified output back into memory twice, so its memory grows with the total section text of the corpus (on the measured cohort the peak RSS was 18.49 times the size of sections_for_annotation.parquet, and its increase over the start of the call 16.14 times). See "Known limitations" in Resumability, Recovery, and Retention.

docs.title: Metadata role
docs.text: This stage can enrich downstream outputs with document-type and processing-stage information.

docs.title: Contributor note
docs.text: Changes here should preserve compatibility with the section parquet contract and should document any new output schema or annotation semantics.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The clean stage normalizes extracted Markdown and evaluates its quality.

docs.title: Main responsibilities
docs.text:
• run the shared OCR analyzer in either clean or debug rendering mode
  • compute text quality and badness metrics
  • detect documents that require OCR reruns
  • update metadata for downstream stage selection

docs.title: Main inputs
docs.text:
• Markdown in markdown/
  • metadata parquet
  • cleaner configuration and thresholds

docs.title: Main outputs
docs.text:
• cleaned Markdown in clean_markdown/
  • debug-marked Markdown under debug/ when debug output is requested
  • debug manifests under debug/:
  • manifest.jsonl
  • page_metrics.jsonl
  • match_index.jsonl
  • summary.json
  • quality metrics and reports
  • metadata updates including OCR-related decisions

docs.title: Why this stage is critical
docs.text:
This stage is the main bridge between extraction and corrective OCR.

It is especially important for Greek corpora because it distinguishes:

  • technically extracted text
  • actually usable Greek text

It also separates two different responsibilities that are easy to conflate:

  • structural cleanup
  • tables, numeric runs, LaTeX collapse, hybrid numbered loops, word repetition
  • quality scoring
  • bad-character metrics
  • suspicious-line metrics
  • OCR rerun recommendations

The stage now uses one shared analyzer for both:

  • debug mode
  • shows exact match placement with <match ...> tags
  • records merged-span match metadata in match_index.jsonl
  • clean mode
  • removes or rewrites those exact same matched regions
  • clean + debug
  • writes pipeline-ready cleaned Markdown and the parallel debug artifacts from the same span plan in one run

docs.title: Important operational outputs
docs.text:
This stage may contribute or update:

  • quality scores
  • filter classifications
  • needs_ocr
  • character-count-based diagnostics
  • processing-stage status

docs.title: Current cleaning policy
docs.text:
The cleaner does not use one generic fuzzy matcher over the whole page. Instead it applies ownership in a fixed order:

  1. tables
  2. numeric
  3. LaTeX
  4. hybrid numbered repetition
  5. shared word repetition

Why this matters:

  • tables can distort the visible text surface for every later pass
  • numeric progressions are often valid cleaner targets but should not be consumed by generic text repetition
  • LaTeX and hybrid passes rely on more specific local structure
  • shared text repetition is therefore safest on the remaining surface only

Table handling is intentionally broader than repetition:

  • sentence_shell_table is dropped
  • empty_table_collapse is dropped
  • repeated_rows is dropped
  • unmatched tables are converted from HTML to GitHub-style Markdown

docs.title: Failure concerns
docs.text:
Typical issues include:

  • missing Rust extension
  • metadata bootstrap issues
  • misleadingly non-empty but low-quality Markdown

docs.title: Contributor note
docs.text:
Changes here affect OCR routing and post-run quality analysis. Treat score and flag semantics as contract-level behavior.

For content-cleaning changes, the exact-output benchmark in tests/test_ocr_golden_pages.py is the main regression lock. Speed work is only acceptable if those outputs remain stable.

docs.title: Extraction failures and page routing
docs.text:
Every metadata row retains extract_status from sidecars/extract/<stem>.json. Legacy sidecars without a status use failure_mode, then the existing parquet status; absent provenance is explicitly unknown. Extraction workers publish status and source page_count for PDFium and Docling, and the controller merges these into parquet. Safe PDFium extraction stays on PDFium above 600 pages.

For PDFs, a problematic, timeout, failed, failure, or error extraction, or missing input Markdown, adds the extract_failed filter reason and sets needs_ocr=True, even if quality metrics are unknown or an old ocr_success flag is present. These rows retain an empty ocr_pages route and a zero ocr_pages_count: OCR uses the whole-document fallback. An empty Markdown file that exists instead goes through the existing is_empty gate.

Valid page-quality sidecars attach ocr_pages and ocr_pages_count to both flagged and unflagged PDFs without promoting the document-level needs_ocr flag. ocr_pages_unflagged_count records selected pages inside unflagged documents in both routing modes. Corpus.ocr() defaults to page_routing='all' for OCR modes: it considers page-quality routes in flagged and unflagged documents. Set page_routing='flagged' explicitly to restrict OCR to cleaner-flagged documents. mode='math_only' performs no OCR and retains its separate flagged-document exclusion policy. A flagged document whose valid page-quality report routes no page is not dispatched (as glossapi run, K5 quality policy P4d); a flagged document without a report keeps the whole-document fallback. Existing completion and skip-list gates continue to apply. Explicit reruns of completed, unflagged documents retain whole-document behavior in flagged mode; only all applies their retained page routes. These counts describe selection, not successful execution.

pua_char_count counts BMP private-use characters U+E000–U+F8FF in the input Markdown. control_char_count counts C0/C1 controls U+0000–U+001F and U+007F–U+009F, excluding normal Markdown whitespace TAB, LF and CR. Both metrics are nullable when Markdown is absent. Page-quality rows expose the same inputs; PUA/control dominance above the symbol-garbage threshold routes sparse corrupt text before the blank-page gate. Counts alone do not establish that every PUA character is erroneous, and the cleaner does not flag an entire document merely because it contains PUA characters.

Text metrics are measured on the markup-free text (K5-A2b, K5A2A-G2): for a layout-labelled Markdown (the safe backend's default) the extract sidecar's markdown_layout.strip record gives the plain text back (glossapi.markdown_layout.markup_free), and the native cleaner report (mojibake_badness_score, percentage_greek, latin_percentage, char_count_no_comments, is_empty), the noise scores (greek_badness_score, polytonic_ratio) and the raw-text measurements (latin_word_shape_rate, pua_char_count, control_char_count, the glyph check below) are taken from it. The cleaned Markdown is still cleaned from the labelled Markdown and keeps its markup. A record that does not describe the file (changed text, another file) is not applied. Docling Markdown has no record and is measured as before. After OCR, clean_ocr measures its OCR profile on the markup-free text and also cleans that text; the edits from its cleaned (labelled) output to that cleaned plain text are kept as a strip record of the cleaned file (a recovery artifact of the clean attempt, or in memory on the legacy profile), and the score-only clean that follows measures the cleaned plain text through it. A score-only pass in a new process without that record falls back to the extract sidecar's record, which describes the cleaned file only when the OCR cleaner left it unchanged.

All-GLYPH text (K5 quality policy P4a): a document whose text is entirely glyph names or unusable glyph codes has no readable characters and is routed to OCR with the filter token glyph_only (needs_ocr=True, reason code clean_glyph_only). "Entirely" means at least 10 glyph-name matches covering at least 90% of the text's non-whitespace characters, measured with the cleaner's own Rule A/B matchers on the raw (markup-free) text (glossapi_rs_cleaner.glyph_residue_counts, native API level 3). The cleaner itself still drops such lines before it scores, so the mojibake score of the cleaned text stays low.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The download stage acquires source documents from parquet-based URL metadata and creates the initial local corpus artifact set.

Prerequisites: the core install does not include the downloader. Install the download package (python install_glossapi.py download) for HTTP downloads. The browser routes (download_mode="auto" escalation and download_mode="browser") need the browser package (python install_glossapi.py browser) and a one-time python -m playwright install chromium, which glossAPI never runs for you.

docs.title: Main responsibilities
docs.text:
• read URL-bearing parquet input
  • download files concurrently
  • route known browser-gated sources through browser-assisted acquisition when configured
  • retain source metadata context
  • avoid refetching previously successful downloads
  • assign stable-enough local filenames for downstream processing

docs.title: Main inputs
docs.text:
• input parquet containing URLs
  • downloader configuration
  • optional prior download result parquet files

docs.title: Main outputs
docs.text:
• downloaded files under downloads/
  • parquet outputs under download_results/
  • log files under logs/

docs.title: Important metadata role
docs.text:
This stage seeds the metadata that later stages build on top of.

That is why original scraping metadata should be preserved rather than discarded after download.

docs.title: Resumability behavior
docs.text:
The downloader supports resume-like behavior by consulting existing result parquet files and skipping already successful URLs.

A rerun of Corpus.download over the same input skips the URLs that already succeeded. The URLs still pending go to the downloader with every column of the input (for example title, or a preassigned filename_base) and the provenance columns (source_row, url_index, collection_slug, source_id, resource_identity), exactly as on the first run. A row resumed after a failure therefore keeps its source fields and its preassigned file name.

A skipped duplicate URL and a failed download have an empty filename. They are kept as separate rows, each with its own URL, error and source fields (see Metadata, artifacts and run diagnostics).

glossapi run downloads through the same downloader but decides what to fetch from the ledger, not from the result parquet files.

This is a major operational feature for large corpora.

docs.title: Failure concerns
docs.text:
Typical issues include:

  • transient network failures
  • rate limiting
  • browser-gated file endpoints that return HTML challenge/interstitial pages
  • viewer-only sources that should fail cleanly instead of being recorded as successful downloads
  • duplicate URLs
  • filename collisions
  • partially completed corpus fetches

docs.title: Public targets only
docs.text: A URL with userinfo (user:pass@) or a credential-named query or fragment field, and any credential setting or header, is refused with credentials_unsupported before a request is built. Hand over protected files as local paths instead.

docs.title: Browser-gated sources
docs.text:
The downloader now distinguishes between:

  • direct file endpoints
  • browser-gated file endpoints
  • viewer-only/document-reader sources

For browser-gated file endpoints:

  • download_mode="auto" probes with direct HTTP and escalates to a browser session when it detects a recoverable interstitial
  • download_mode="browser" goes directly to the browser-assisted path
  • download_policy_file=... can route known domains or URL patterns to the correct path without probing every file

Browser-assisted mode is designed for retrievable file endpoints, not for sources that only expose page images, tiles, HTML/SVG re-rendering, or DRM-wrapped readers.

docs.title: Session reuse
docs.text:
Browser-assisted mode reuses cached browser session state per domain so multiple files from the same protected source do not need a fresh browser bootstrap every time.

This keeps the browser as a session-bootstrap resource rather than the main downloader.

docs.title: Contributor note
docs.text:
Any change to filename assignment or result parquet structure can have downstream impact on:

  • extraction discovery
  • metadata joins
  • rerun behavior

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The export stage reshapes processed corpus data into downstream-friendly formats such as JSONL and aggregated metadata views.

docs.title: Main responsibilities
docs.text:
• read processed metadata and stage outputs
  • aggregate chunked and unchunked document information
  • emit export-oriented records for downstream consumers

docs.title: Main inputs
docs.text:
• metadata parquet
  • section or text outputs depending on export mode
  • chunk-aware naming and aggregation logic

docs.title: Main outputs
docs.text:
• exported JSONL or related downstream formats

In a streaming run (Corpus.run(), glossapi run) the export stage writes export.jsonl in the corpus folder and records, for every selected document version, whether it was included or omitted and why. glossapi report (the census) and glossapi report --why read those decisions, and they count a version as included only when the export generation wrote its record. After OCR this still holds: the cleaned text produced after OCR is bound to the planned document version, so the census, --why and export.jsonl agree.

docs.title: Page, formula and code counters
docs.text: The exported page_count, formula_total and code_total carry no measurement method. They come from the first readable metrics file of the document (json/metrics/<stem>.metrics.json, else json/metrics/<stem>.per_page.metrics.json); formula_total and code_total add up the per-page counts in that file, and a page without a count adds 0. Without a metrics file the metadata row's existing value is kept, and formula_total/code_total become 0 when that is missing too. So 0 can mean "not measured". The ledger records which file was used and labels the method unknown_if_not_reported_by_metrics.

docs.title: Why this stage matters
docs.text:
Export is where many earlier assumptions become visible:

  • whether document identity is stable
  • whether chunked outputs can be reconstructed correctly
  • whether metadata remains coherent after reruns and recovery

docs.title: Contributor note
docs.text: Changes to export logic often reveal hidden assumptions in the rest of the pipeline. Document those assumptions explicitly rather than leaving them embedded in naming or aggregation code.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The extraction stage converts source files into Markdown and optional structured byproducts such as Docling JSON.

docs.title: Main responsibilities
docs.text:
• locate source files for processing
  • choose extraction backend behavior
  • produce Markdown
  • optionally emit structured JSON artifacts
  • balance throughput against stability

docs.title: Main inputs
docs.text:
• files in downloads/ or explicitly provided file paths
  • extraction configuration
  • backend selection and accelerator settings

docs.title: Main outputs
docs.text:
• repaired PDF sidecars in repaired_pdfs/<stem>.pdf when eligible
  • font-repair metadata in the canonical download-results parquet
  • Markdown in markdown/
  • optional JSON artifacts in json/
  • stage logs and timeout/problematic-file traces

docs.title: Key design point
docs.text:
This stage is where the Docling throughput strategy meets the pipeline's stability constraints.

It should be understood as both:

  • a text extraction stage
  • an operational risk management stage

docs.title: Backend semantics
docs.text:
The extraction logic distinguishes between safer extraction behavior and Docling-focused behavior.

This matters because Docling is powerful, but not equally stable under all batching and corpus conditions.

docs.title: Layout-aware Markdown (layout v2, core install)
docs.text:
The safe backend (the default phase1_backend='auto'/'safe') writes layout-aware Markdown without Docling: the PDFium plain text in plain order, cut into blocks and labelled by layout v2 (glossapi.markdown_layout, Rust in glossapi_rs_pdfrepair). Labels never change the text and nothing is re-ordered. It needs only the core install (pypdfium2 and the glossapi_rs_pdfrepair extension at native API level 3); the layout extra and its docling alias are not involved.

GLOSSAPI_MARKDOWN_LAYOUT selects the safe backend's Markdown: layout_v2 (default, extract stage contract 3; 2 was K5-A2a's sidecar without the strip record) or plain (the plain pages, byte for byte as before; contract 2: hash-bound plain_pages physical page offsets in the sidecar). The value is part of the extract stage identity.

Rendering rules (glossapi-layout-md/1, markdown_layout/render.py):

block Markdown page separator one blank line between non-blank pages, as before (page offsets are in the metadata) between blocks of a page one blank line (replaces the block's original whitespace separator) title # text section_header level n # x min(6, n + 1), a space, the text (newlines inside the heading become spaces) list_item - text, unless the text already starts with -, *, +, 1. or 1) and a space caption, footnote, table, picture, formula a <!-- caption --> (etc.) line, then the text page_header, page_footer a <!-- page-header --> / <!-- page-footer --> line, then the text (kept) paragraph, unlabelled page the text

Text is never escaped. Deleting the added markup and restoring each block's original separator gives the page text byte for byte. A page is emitted unlabelled (its text unchanged) when it has no char table, no text layer, a page box or font size outside the input contract (layout_input_rejected) or the labeller fails on it.

The extract sidecar (sidecars/extract/<stem>.json) carries markdown_layout: schema, rules, reader (native or python), status (labelled, partial, unlabelled, unavailable), per-page and per-block code-point offsets into the Markdown with labels and levels, label counts, labeller warnings, rejected pages and the document context, and strip: the edits that undo the markup ([start, end, original] code-point spans: each prefix deleted, each block separator and each heading newline restored) with the length and sha256 of the Markdown it describes and the sha256 of the plain text it gives back. markdown_layout.markup_free applies it (checking both hashes; an appended OCR supplement after the native pages is kept), and the cleaner measures every text metric on that markup-free text, so the metrics and routing decisions of the default mode equal the plain mode's (K5-A2b, K5A2A-G2). The cleaned Markdown keeps the markup. In Corpus.run and the stage adapters the sidecar is the clean stage's bound layout_metadata input (clean contract 2 in the default mode, 1 in plain mode).

The sidecar also carries decode_status for the safe backend (K5 quality policy P4b, both Markdown modes): one entry per page, from the native content-stream check of the file PDFium read (glossapi_rs_pdfrepair.page_decode_status_json; PDFium's own error state is not a signal). partial: a content stream of the page, or of a Form XObject it draws, or the ToUnicode CMap of a font the page selects (Tf, in its own streams or a drawn form), failed to decode or ended before its end marker; the page keeps the readable text PDFium extracts. FlateDecode, LZWDecode, RunLengthDecode, ASCIIHex and ASCII85 are decoded. An RC4-encrypted document whose user password is empty (an owner-password document, which PDFium opens) is decrypted for this check only (analysis and font repair still refuse encrypted documents). Annotation appearance streams are not checked: PDFium's text page does not read them. Font programs are not checked. unknown: the check could not run or decide (stale or missing native module, a document the native parser cannot open, such as one encrypted with AES or with a user password, or one whose cross-reference table PDFium has to rebuild, a page count that differs from PDFium's, an unavailable page, an unreadable stream object, a filter the check does not implement); reason or reasons say why. complete: the check ran and found no decode failure. The same list is in the ledger's page coverage (page_coverage.decode_status). The status never routes a page by itself.

Reading: each page is loaded once. layout_v2_read_document opens the document with Rust-owned PDFium handles and returns each page's text (exactly get_text_range()) and char table from the same text page. If the native reader is unavailable (LayoutV2ReaderUnavailable) the text comes from pypdfium2 as before and the char tables from the Python reference reader (same bytes, slower); a document or page the native reader cannot open is read the pypdfium2 way, with exactly pypdfium2's exceptions. A missing or stale extension gives the plain Markdown.

Reader threat model (K5 policy P7): Documents and public argument values are untrusted; the Python runtime, installed dependencies and executable caller code are trusted. The wrapper validates arguments and preserves native handle ownership and lifetime. Dependency replacement, forged ctypes state and uncoordinated library teardown are unsupported. All PDFium users, initialization and destruction require process-wide coordination; the reader's mutex and GIL do not serialize external ctypes calls. Identity checks and self-tests detect accidental incompatibility, not malicious substitution. This boundary does not sandbox PDFium or guarantee unlimited resource availability.

Coordination: every glossAPI module that opens a PDF with pypdfium2 does so under glossapi.pdfium_guard (one re-entrant lock per process, reset in a forked child), and every native read takes the same lock, so no two PDFium users overlap in one process. glossAPI never initializes or destroys PDFium: pypdfium2 does at import and at exit.

Docling stays available through phase1_backend='docling' and the layout extra (alias docling) for what layout v2 does not replace:

capability core (layout v2) layout extra (Docling 2.81) headings, lists, captions, footnotes, furniture labels yes (labels on the plain order) yes (Docling layout model) text source PDFium plain text docling-parse text (transliterates TeX-encoded Greek) table structure (rows, cells, Markdown tables) no (table text marked <!-- table -->) yes math/code enrichment no yes (formula_enrichment, code_enrichment) Docling JSON (json/<stem>.docling.json) no yes (export_doc_json) non-PDF conversion no yes GPU not needed optional

docs.title: Font repair pre-pass
docs.text:
Corpus.extract(..., repair_fonts=True) enables CPU ToUnicode repair by default for both the safe and Docling backends. Set repair_fonts=False to extract the original text layer. Each file's extraction worker analyzes its PDF immediately before conversion; a repairable or mixed document with at least one eligible font receives a repaired copy in <output_dir>/repaired_pdfs/<stem>.pdf. The extractor opens that copy. Original PDFs in downloads/ stay unchanged, and Markdown names, resume keys and metadata retain the original filename/stem. Non-PDF inputs bypass repair.

An existing repaired_pdfs/<stem>.pdf is never reused: a newer modification time does not prove that the copy was made from the current source bytes, so each extraction analyses the source and repairs it again (the repair is deterministic, so the same source gives the same bytes). The ledger paths (Corpus.run(), glossapi run) reuse work by the source hashes they record instead. Ordinary skip_existing=True resume still skips completed Markdown entirely; skip_existing=False re-extracts and repairs again.

The pre-pass uses at most half of the existing per-file extraction timeout, reserving the rest for extraction. Its elapsed time is deducted from the shared budget, including chunked conversion and retries. Analysis/repair failures and pre-pass timeouts fall back to the original PDF and record error plus the message in the extract sidecar and parquet's existing extract_error column. The stage continues. Docling retains its existing native timeout behavior; converters without native timeout support cannot enforce the extraction portion of the deadline. POSIX main-thread signal timers bound the pre-pass without an extra process pool. Unsupported timer contexts fall back with error; native C calls may delay signal delivery until they return to Python.

Workers write sidecars/extract/<stem>.json; the controller merges these four columns into the canonical metadata parquet after extraction:

Column Type / default Meaning font_repair_status string / skipped repaired, not_needed (consistent), unsupported, no_text_layer, error, or skipped (disabled/unprocessed). font_repair_fonts int / 0 Number of fonts repaired. font_repair_valid_rate_before float / null Dictionary validity over the original PDF's first 20 pages. font_repair_valid_rate_after float / null Dictionary validity over the repaired PDF's first 20 pages, or the unchanged original.

Configure GLOSSAPI_GREEK_WORDLIST with a local UTF-8 word list to compute rates with extract_text_stats. Missing/unreadable dictionaries or metric failures leave rates null. Each repaired PDF gets one INFO line with its stem, font count and available before→after rates. The final summary counts statuses for the stage's selected PDFs, including previously completed files on resume.

docs.title: Failure concerns
docs.text:
Typical issues include:

  • Docling crashes
  • hangs or timeouts
  • worker poisoning after a bad file
  • partial progress during corpus-scale processing

docs.title: Fatal skiplist
docs.text: The fatal skiplist holds files a worker failed on; a later direct Corpus.extract call skips them (a Corpus.run() decides from the ledger and does not read the skiplist). When every multi-GPU worker has exited, the files still queued were never attempted: they are recorded as workers_exhausted_unattempted and are not added to the skiplist, so the next Corpus.extract processes them.

docs.title: Recovery concerns
docs.text:
Recovery should preserve:

  • successful Markdown already produced
  • visibility into failed documents
  • enough information to avoid repeating the same crash pattern blindly

docs.title: Contributor note
docs.text: Any change to batch policy, backend selection, or output naming should be treated as an architectural change, not just a local refactor.

docs.title: OCR remediation
docs.text:
Run extraction and cleaning first, then call corpus.ocr(mode="ocr_bad"). The default is the pinned external Greek R8+x1 plugin. Install it with python install_glossapi.py ocr --device cpu (or mps / cuda126 / cuda132). Explicit ocr_options still select a configured plugin; there is no silent engine fallback. glossapi run --stages ocr,export also supports this default and routes only pages flagged by page quality.

The toolkit registers glossapi = "greekocr.deploy.docling_plugin.docling_plugin" in the Docling docling entry-point group. Docling loads ocr_engines() with allow_external_plugins=True; the engine owns its options, model files and inference.

page_routing="all" (the default for the OCR modes) uses the page policy of glossapi run: every page that page quality routes is OCRed, in documents the cleaner flagged and in documents it did not. page_routing="flagged" restricts OCR to the documents the cleaner flagged (needs_ocr), the default before K4g. mode="math_only" performs no OCR and by default still skips only cleaner-flagged documents. Ranges are inclusive, one-based physical pages. A cleaner-flagged document whose page quality routed no page is not OCRed by Corpus.ocr in either setting, as glossapi run keeps its extracted text (ocr_not_routed, cause flagged_without_routed_pages; K5 quality policy P4d). A document without a page-quality report keeps document-level routing: the OCR stage's own page quality picks its pages. A document whose native text layer is entirely glyph names (the cleaner's glyph_only token, K5 quality policy P4a) is OCRed whole, in Corpus.ocr and in glossapi run alike: page quality v4 does not route such non-Greek symbol pages, so the OCR stage's glyph check selects every page (decision route: glyph_only). Skip-list and completed-document filtering still apply. Partial OCR replaces selected physical pages in place, without adding page markers. The default extractor's markdown_layout.pages offsets are checked against its strip record's full Markdown hash; plain extraction records equivalent hash-bound plain_pages offsets. Blank pages keep their physical page numbers. Missing, stale or unusable offsets retain the original and append the existing supplement; page_replacement_fallback_reason in the OCR metrics explains the fallback. Legacy explicit page boundaries and checked Docling provenance remain supported. The latest replacement per physical page is retained on reruns. The immutable native snapshot and committed OCR page state allow a killed attempt to restart.

Replacement writes sidecars/ocr_layout/<stem>.json: a new hash-bound strip of the assembled Markdown. Only retained native markup is stripped for metrics; OCR text remains the engine's text. Both the run DAG and compatibility cleaner bind this provenance, including the post-OCR cleanup and scoring passes.

OCR attempts use an absolute deadline of max(600, min(7200, 120 + 45*N)) seconds, where N is the routed page count (bounded by max_pages). The scheduler computes it before dispatch and records the policy in ocr_deadline attempt settings. A supplied ocr.timeout_seconds overrides it. The deadline remains fixed during an attempt and the worker watchdog terminates hangs; an active attempt cannot renew its budget.

Routing v4 remains the default. The existing rule_profile switch also accepts experimental v5 (settings.page_quality.rule_profile in run, or page_quality(..., rule_profile="v5")). It preserves v4 and adds measured English validity on Latin-dominant text layers with at least 50 characters: less than 40% recognized Latin tokens selects OCR. Every effective threshold, rate and dictionary identity is recorded and replayable. The pinned SCOWL en_US Hunspell surface entries are bundled under their MIT/BSD terms, with the full notice in data/wordlists/LICENSE.en_US. English vocabulary cannot certify all Latin-script languages, technical notation or Greek hidden behind Latin font encodings; qualification and rendered-page review determine whether this profile is suitable for a corpus.

Experimental v6 extends this measurement to English, French, German, Italian Spanish and Portuguese. It chooses one language per page by the greatest dictionary token hit rate (ties: en, fr, de, it, es, pt), then applies the same 40% validity bar. The additional Moby Language II vocabularies are public-domain surface lists; Portuguese uses OWN-PT one-word lemmas (CC BY 4.0) plus MIT function words; source hashes, normalization and notices ship beside the lists. They add no runtime dependency or language model. Rates are exact vocabulary measurements, not probabilities or proof of the page's physical language.

The v6 check requires at least 50 characters, 10 Latin tokens and 80% Latin letters among Greek plus Latin letters. Shorter and substantially mixed-script pages retain v4 routing; Greek validity is never measured with a Latin list. All candidate-language rates, the selected language, token count, applicability and guards are recorded per page. ORP-style Latin-encoded Greek can still fail all vocabularies, which is useful for bad-layer detection but is not evidence that the physical page is English. v4 stays the default; v5 remains available with its original English-only behavior.

Successful OCR updates canonical Markdown, metrics, text, ocr_success, needs_ocr, extraction_mode="docling", and OCR artifact pointers/hashes in parquet, then refreshes the OCR cleaner and score-only cleaner.

mode="math_only" continues to use existing Docling JSON. See math enrichment and migration.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The section stage splits Markdown documents into structural units suitable for classification and downstream analysis.

docs.title: Main responsibilities
docs.text:
• select eligible documents for sectioning
  • parse Markdown structure
  • emit section-level parquet data

docs.title: Main inputs
docs.text:
• Markdown artifacts
  • metadata indicating which files are acceptable for downstream processing

docs.title: Main outputs
docs.text: • section parquet outputs under sections/

docs.title: Selection semantics
docs.text:
Corpus.section() sections the documents Corpus.clean() selected in the same Corpus object (good_files). Without that list it selects from the metadata parquet: rows whose filter is ok or empty, or whose ocr_success is true (and, if none match, rows whose legacy extraction column is good). If nothing is selected, it falls back to every Markdown file and records section_legacy_all_fallback. In a streaming run only the run's planned documents are sectioned.

That means sectioning is downstream of quality gating, not independent from it.

docs.title: Global section IDs
docs.text: The numeric section id values in sections_for_annotation.parquet follow the order in which the filesystem lists markdown/ (os.listdir, not sorted). A streaming run records that listing in the ledger as an input of the sections publication, so the IDs of a run can be traced, but the same files can get different IDs on a filesystem that lists them in another order. Treat id as a compatibility field; the ledger keeps stable private section keys.

docs.title: Failure concerns
docs.text:
Typical issues include:

  • no usable markdown available
  • metadata selection mismatches
  • malformed markdown structure

docs.title: Contributor note
docs.text: If section selection rules change, the documentation must also explain how eligibility is determined from metadata and artifacts.

docs.title: Compatibility And Regression Matrix
docs.text:
This document defines the release-validation matrix for the Greek OCR toolkit integration, Docling upgrades and other changes to the documented pipeline contracts. The current status of each gate is at the end of this page.

It is not a generic unit-test list. It is a contract-based validation plan tied to the documented pipeline behavior.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This matrix applies to changes in:

  • external OCR integration
  • no-stub enforcement
  • installation simplification
  • Docling dependency upgrades
  • page-level reevaluation experiments

docs.title: Validation policy
docs.text:
Release validation for these contracts must use:

  • real PDFs
  • real Docling
  • real external OCR engine
  • real GPUs where the code path requires them

Developer-only tests may still use mocks or lightweight stubs for fast iteration, but those do not satisfy release gates.

docs.title: L0: Install and import sanity
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • prove the supported environments install cleanly and that removed components are truly gone

Typical inputs:

  • fresh venv
  • supported Python version

docs.title: L1: Lightweight smoke corpus
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • prove the baseline end-to-end flow still works on the small repo corpus

Typical inputs:

  • samples/lightweight_pdf_corpus/

docs.title: L2: Real-PDF contract validation
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • prove the documented artifacts and metadata contracts still hold on real documents

Typical inputs:

  • real PDFs from a representative sample

docs.title: L3: Multi-GPU and operational recovery
docs.text:
Multi-GPU OCR is a target that has not been qualified; the external OCR plugin runs on one device.

Purpose:

  • prove the runtime behavior remains correct under parallel execution and rerun conditions

Typical inputs:

  • multiple real PDFs
  • at least two visible GPUs

docs.title: L4: Comparative corpus evaluation
docs.text:
Purpose:

  • compare baseline and changed behavior on a real evaluation slice

Typical inputs:

  • real corpus slice such as the Pergamos sample

docs.title: Mandatory invariants
docs.text:
The following must remain true unless a change explicitly revises the contract and updates the docs:

  • canonical Markdown is written to markdown/<stem>.md
  • Docling JSON artifacts are emitted when requested
  • cleaner output still drives needs_ocr
  • OCR remains selective: only pages that page quality routes (page_routing="all", the default) or only documents the cleaner flagged (page_routing="flagged")
  • the ledger corpus.sqlite3 is the durable record of a streaming run; the metadata parquet stays the compatibility record of the phase methods
  • reruns skip completed work unless forced
  • skiplist semantics remain explicit and stable
  • no production path silently falls back to stub OCR

docs.title: Install and runtime compatibility
docs.text:
What to prove:

  • supported environment installs cleanly
  • unsupported/removed OCR components are not required
  • Python floor matches actual upstream dependencies

Critical checks:

  • packaging metadata uses a supported Python minimum
  • setup docs expose only supported install paths
  • removal of the old OCR integration does not leave dead GlossAPI imports or entrypoints

docs.title: Extraction contract
docs.text:
What to prove:

  • Phase-1 still produces canonical Markdown
  • Docling extraction still produces JSON artifacts when requested
  • metrics continue to be written where downstream stages expect them

Artifacts to check:

  • markdown/<stem>.md
  • json/<stem>.docling.json(.zst)
  • json/<stem>.formula_index.jsonl when requested
  • json/metrics/<stem>.metrics.json
  • json/metrics/<stem>.per_page.metrics.json

docs.title: Cleaning and Greek-quality routing
docs.text:
What to prove:

  • cleaner still computes routing decisions required for selective OCR
  • Greek-text validation remains first-class rather than incidental cleanup

Fields to check in metadata parquet:

  • needs_ocr
  • filter
  • Greek-quality and badness-related fields currently emitted by the cleaner

docs.title: external plugin OCR contract
docs.text:
What to prove:

  • OCR remediation uses a configured external Docling engine
  • no-stub enforcement is real
  • recovered documents update metadata correctly

Required environment behavior:

  • real model weights present
  • real CLI/runtime path present

Negative checks:

  • no markdown contains placeholder stub markers
  • no OCR pass succeeds after an engine failure
  • no removed OCR backend is referenced during final validation

docs.title: Formula and code enrichment
docs.text:
What to prove:

  • if retained, enrichment still works with the upgraded Docling stack
  • if later removed, the removal is justified by evaluation rather than convenience

Checks:

  • enriched Markdown is generated where expected
  • json/<stem>.latex_map.jsonl remains coherent when enrichment is enabled
  • metadata updates for math enrichment still work

docs.title: Section, annotate, and export contracts
docs.text:
What to prove:

  • downstream stages still consume the extraction outputs
  • output layout and metadata structure remain compatible with the documented pipeline

Artifacts to check:

  • sections/sections_for_annotation.parquet
  • classified_sections.parquet
  • fully_annotated_sections.parquet
  • exported JSONL shards and related metadata

docs.title: Resumability and operational recovery
docs.text:
What to prove:

  • reruns still honor completion state
  • skiplist semantics remain intact
  • multi-worker failures remain visible and recoverable

Checks:

  • default rerun skips completed items
  • explicit force/reprocess reruns the intended items
  • problematic stems are persisted and not silently lost

docs.title: Comparative evaluation set
docs.text:
Suggested real-world slice:

  • lightweight corpus for smoke validation
  • representative real PDFs spanning:
  • short documents
  • medium documents
  • long documents
  • structure-rich documents
  • math-heavy documents where applicable

For current local evaluation work, a Pergamos sample manifest has been prepared outside the repo and can be used as the L3/L4 real-PDF slice.

docs.title: Gate order
docs.text:
For a change that touches these contracts, run gates in this order:

  1. ENV-*
  2. EXT-*
  3. CLN-*
  4. OCR-*
  5. MTH-*
  6. SEC-*, ANN-*, EXP-*
  7. RES-*, SKP-*, GPU-*
  8. CMP-*

This keeps low-level compatibility failures from being confused with downstream quality regressions.

docs.text:
The external OCR migration is complete: the pinned Greek OCR toolkit is the only supported OCR engine, the removed engines and install modes are gone, and Docling is an optional backend. The status of each gate group for 0.2.0:

A fresh install must still be checked on each target platform and Python version.
